The five-fold repetition is the chapter's deliberate protest-formula refrain — the brothers' self-defense against the accusation of being *meraglim* (spies, the chapter's counter-keyword).** // **The lexeme.** The adjective *ken* III (כֵּן, 'right, true, honest, upright') is morphologically the homonymous form of *ken* I ('thus, so', the adverb of manner) and *ken* II ('base, pedestal', the noun) — three homonyms in HALOT distinguished by syntactic-role and context. *Ken* III in its predicative-adjective sense is well-attested: 'right, true' applied to speech (Num 27:7; 36:5: *ken benot Tzelofchad doverot*, 'the daughters of Tzelofchad speak right'; Exod 10:29 *ken dibbarta*; 2 Kgs 7:9 *lo ken anachnu osim*, 'we are not doing right'; Eccl 8:10 *lo ken*); to action (Prov 11:19 *ken tzedaqah le-chayim*, 'so righteousness tends to life'); to attestation (Job 5:27 *hineh zot chaqarnuha ken hi*, 'lo this, we have searched it, so it is'). The substantival-plural-of-persons sense *kenim* ('honest men, persons-of-integrity') is RARE — Gen 42 is the principal locus (the five chapter-internal occurrences plus its retelling-recurrence) — and is itself a chapter-specific deployment of the lexeme: the brothers are using the adjective as a noun, applying it to themselves as a class. The cross-corpus substantival-plural sense recurs at 2 Sam 14:18 (Avshalom's intermediary woman to David) and a few wisdom-attestations; the chapter-internal five-fold deployment dominates. // **The chapter's protest-formula structure.** The five occurrences form a literary structure: v 11 the brothers' initial self-designation (*kenim anachnu*); v 19 Yosef's conditional acceptance of the self-designation (*im kenim atem*, 'if ye be honest men'); v 31 the brothers retelling to Ya'aqov (*kenim anachnu*, 'we are honest men'); v 33 the brothers retelling Yosef's verification-condition (*be-zot eda ki kenim atem*, 'hereby shall I know that ye are honest men'); v 34 Yosef's closing conditional (*ki kenim atem*, 'that ye are honest men'). The refrain binds the brothers' protest, Yosef's test, the retelling to Ya'aqov, and the test-condition into a single rhetorical structure. The chapter's dramatic irony is sharp: the brothers' self-designation as *kenim* is precisely what the chapter is testing — whether they are honest about *what they did to Yosef*, the past that the v 21 confession is about to expose. The Gen 42:21 confession (*aval ashemim anachnu al achinu*) is the chapter's answer to its own *kenim*-claim: in the matter of Yosef, the brothers are NOT *kenim* but *ashemim* — guilty, not honest. The lexical contrast *kenim* (vv 11, 19, 31, 33, 34) ↔ *ashemim* (v 21) is one of the chapter's deepest literary-theological structures. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV 'true men' (the archaic English register that retains the moral-uprightness force of *ken* — 'true' in the sense of 'morally true, of integrity', not the modern 'factually true'); NJPS / NRSV / Alter 'honest men' (modern register, sacrificing the *ken* etymological resonance for clarity). The ASV-baseline 'true men' is preserved for two reasons: (i) consistency across the five occurrences (the refrain is preserved); (ii) the etymological resonance with *ken*'s moral-uprightness sense (the archaic 'true' carries 'morally true' more clearly than modern 'true'). // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-internal five-fold refrain; the substantival-plural-of-persons *kenim* sense is chapter-specific (the adjective *ken* in its predicative-adjective sense is cross-corpus, but the substantival 'honest men' deployment as a self-designating protest-formula is chapter-singular); → **OVERLAY**. The lemma's cross-corpus reach in other senses is governed elsewhere; the chapter-specific protest-refrain is here. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit (adjective *ken* III, substantival-plural form); (b) the chapter's five-fold deployment is textually verifiable; (c) the *kenim* ↔ *ashemim* lexical contrast is grammatically explicit; (d) the ASV-baseline 'true men' is the direct rendering. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *ken* III; BDB p. 467; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 107; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 518-519; on the *kenim* / *ashemim* lexical contrast: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 242.

terms.translit: mishmar (v 17, 'ward'); beit mishmarkhem (v 19, 'your prison-house')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine singular (mishmar — 'guard, custody, place of detention'); in construct beit mishmar — 'house of custody, prison-house'
terms.literal: mishmar — the general 'guard / custody / place of detention'; beit mishmar — 'house of [the] custody', the construct-noun-phrase 'prison-house'
terms.standardEnglish: ward (ASV/KJV — archaic register); guardhouse / prison (NJPS); prison (NRSV); ward / prison (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: ward (v 17) / prison-house (v 19 in the beit mishmarkhem construct) — ASV-baseline; the chapter's mishmar terminology distinguished from the Gen 39-40 beit ha-sohar in commentary
terms.rationale: **Genesis 42 deploys *mishmar* (v 17) and the construct *beit mishmarkhem* (v 19) as the chapter's terms for the place where Yosef detains the brothers (v 17, the initial three-day detention of all ten) and the place where Shim'on will be held (v 19, the conditional-pending-Binyamin detention). The terminology is distinct from the Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar* (the 'round-house / prison' that is governed by the central [`beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house`](#beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house) entry); whether the *mishmar* of Gen 42 names the same facility as the *beit ha-sohar* of Gen 39-40 or a different one is undecidable from the texts alone.** // **The lexeme.** The noun *mishmar* (from the root *sh-m-r* 'to guard, keep, watch') has three documented senses: (i) the **guarding-act** (a watch, a guard-duty: 2 Chr 8:14 *mishmerot* — 'guard-divisions'; Neh 7:3); (ii) the **guarded persons** (those in custody: Gen 40:3-4, 7 — Yosef and the cupbearer/baker held in the *mishmar* of the *sar ha-tabbachim*; Gen 41:10; 42:17, 19; Lev 24:12; Num 15:34); (iii) the **guarding-personnel** (the guards themselves: Neh 4:3, 9; 7:3 [MT 13:30]). The sense at Gen 42:17 is (ii) — the place of custody / detention. The construct *beit mishmar* ('house of custody') at v 19 specifies the building / facility — the construct-form *beit + noun* is the standard 'building-of-X' construction (cf. *beit ha-sohar*, *beit ha-bor* — 'house of the prison', 'house of the pit'). // **The Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar* / Gen 40 *mishmar* relation.** The central entry [`beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house`](#beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house) governs the *beit ha-sohar* — the Gen 39-40 Egyptian prison (likely a fortress-prison; the Egyptian *sohar* possibly from Eg. *s-h-r-y* 'fortress-tower'). Within Gen 40 the same facility is called both *beit ha-sohar* (vv 3, 5) AND *mishmar* (vv 3, 4, 7 — the cupbearer and baker placed in the *mishmar*; Yosef the *na'ar* serving them). The Gen 40 dual-naming establishes that *mishmar* can name the same facility as *beit ha-sohar*. Gen 42 uses only *mishmar* / *beit mishmar* (not *beit ha-sohar*), suggesting that the editor / narrator either: (a) names the same Egyptian prison-facility (the Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar*) using the alternate *mishmar* terminology — consistent with Gen 40's dual-naming; (b) names a different facility — perhaps a separate detention-area at Yosef's official residence, distinct from the prison Yosef himself was kept in; (c) the lexical-variation is stylistic and not referential. Sarna and Westermann both treat the Gen 42 *mishmar* as functionally the Egyptian prison; the question is undecidable from the texts alone. The English translation cannot recover the question and renders the Hebrew's lexical-variation: *mishmar* → 'ward' (v 17); *beit mishmar* → 'prison-house' (v 19). // **The three-day detention.** Gen 42:17 places the brothers in the *mishmar* for *sheloshet yamim* ('three days'). The three-day period is a marked literary threshold across the corpus: Gen 22:4 (the Aqedah's three days to Moriyah); Gen 40:12, 13, 18, 19, 20 (the cupbearer/baker dreams' three days, the *sar ha-mashqim*'s restoration and the *sar ha-ofim*'s execution both at three days; the dreams' three-day pivot); Gen 42:17 (the brothers' three-day detention); Exod 5:3 (the three-day wilderness journey); Josh 1:11; 2:16, 22; 3:2; 9:16; 2 Sam 1:2; 1 Kgs 12:5; Esth 4:16 (Esther's fast); Jonah 2:1 (Jonah in the fish). The three-day threshold marks transition from one state to another — captivity to resolution, dream to interpretation, journey to destination. The Gen 42:17 three-day detention is itself the threshold between the brothers' arrest and Yosef's conditional release. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-internal *mishmar* / *beit mishmar* terminology; the cross-corpus *mishmar* lexeme is multivalent and broadly distributed (governed by other contexts when those texts are translated); the chapter-specific deployment-as-Egyptian-detention-vocabulary, distinct from Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar*, is here. The cross-reference to the central [`beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house`](#beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house) documents the relation. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the lexeme's multivalent sense-range is direct but the chapter-specific reading is interpretive; (b) the Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar* / Gen 40 *mishmar* same-or-different-facility question is undecidable; (c) the 'ward' / 'prison-house' rendering is the ASV-baseline but the choice between the lexemes preserves Hebrew's lexical-variation. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *mishmar*; BDB p. 1038; TDOT IX:281-285; NIDOTTE 4:191-193; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 291; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 109; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 521; on the three-day-threshold motif: G. F. Hasel 'The Significance of the Cosmology in Genesis 1' AUSS 10 (1972) 1-20; on the *mishmar* / *beit ha-sohar* relation: D. B. Redford *A Study of the Biblical Story of Joseph* VTSup 20, 1970 pp. 17-19.

terms.translit: va-yakkirem (Hiphil 3ms perf w/ 3mp suff, 'and he recognised them'); va-yitnakker (Hithpael 3ms perf, 'and he made himself strange / disguised himself / feigned to be a stranger') — paired in a single verse at Gen 42:7
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, in paired Hiphil (recognise / identify) and Hithpael (make oneself strange / feign-unrecognisability) stems
terms.literal: va-yakkirem — and he recognised / identified them; va-yitnakker — and he made himself strange / disguised himself unto them, feigned not to be the one they would have known
terms.standardEnglish: knew them ... made himself strange unto them (ASV/KJV); recognized them ... acted like a stranger toward them (NJPS); recognized them ... but disguised himself (NRSV); recognized them ... feigned to be a stranger (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: knew them ... made himself strange unto them (ASV-baseline preserved; the Hiphil/Hithpael paired-deployment as the recognition-motif culmination documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:7 stages the chapter's recognition-motif at its culmination by deploying the root *nakar* (נכר) in two opposite stems back-to-back within a single verse: the Hiphil *va-yakkirem* ('and he recognised them' — the same Hiphil that Gen 37:32-33 used at the *haker-na* / *va-yakkirah* exchange between the brothers and Ya'aqov) and the Hithpael *va-yitnakker* ('and he made himself strange / disguised himself / feigned to be a stranger'). The juxtaposition of the recognition-verb and its anti-form within a single verse is rare in the HB and pointed: the verb of recognition is the very verb whose Hithpael Yosef adopts to conceal himself.** // **The Hithpael of *nakar*.** The Hithpael of *n-k-r* ('to make oneself strange / unrecognisable / feign-the-strangeness-of-a-stranger') is rare; the only other HB occurrence of the Hithpael in this specific sense is **1 Kgs 14:5-6** — the prophet Achiyah of Shilo, blind in his old age, is told by YHWH that Yarov'am's wife is coming to inquire of him about their sick child: *ve-hi mitnakkerah* ('and she will make herself strange / will be in disguise', v 5). Yarov'am has sent his wife in disguise to receive an oracle about their son's fate. Achiyah, alerted by YHWH despite his blindness, addresses her at her arrival: *boi eshet Yarov'am, lammah zeh at mitnakkerah* ('come in, wife of Yarov'am; why dost thou feign to be another?', v 6). The 1 Kgs 14:5-6 scene is structurally parallel to Gen 42:7: in both, a person of authority is approached by someone who *should* recognise them but who has been deceived by the visitor's disguise; in both, the addressed party (Achiyah / Yosef) is in fact aware of the visitor's identity and disguise. The verbal parallel is sharp: *mitnakkerah* (1 Kgs 14:5) / *va-yitnakker* (Gen 42:7). The two occurrences exhaust the HB's Hithpael-of-*nakar* in the feigning-unrecognisability sense. // **The chapter's culmination of the Gen 27 / 37 / 38 recognition-arc.** The recognition-motif binds the patriarchal narratives: (a) **Gen 27:23** *ve-lo hikkiro* ('and he recognised him not' — the blind Yitzchaq failing to identify the disguised Ya'aqov, the deception by exploiting recognition's failure); (b) **Gen 37:32-33** *haker-na* / *va-yakkirah* (the brothers' bloodied-tunic deception of Ya'aqov, the deception by demanding recognition); (c) **Gen 38:25-26** *haker-na le-mi* / *va-yakker Yehudah* (Tamar's pledge-items to Yehudah, the deception caught by demanding recognition); (d) **Gen 42:7-8** *va-yakkirem ... va-yitnakker ... ve-hem lo hikkiruhu* (Yosef's controlled recognition combined with concealed identity, the culmination-and-reversal: the brothers, who once exploited Ya'aqov's misrecognition of a bloodied tunic, are themselves misrecognising the brother they sold). The four-stage *nakar*-arc resolves at Gen 42:7-8 with the chapter's exact role-reversal: Yosef holds the recognition-knowledge that Ya'aqov in Gen 27 lacked, and uses it to *feign* the non-recognition that the brothers in Gen 37 created. The Hithpael *va-yitnakker* is the structural counterpart of Gen 27's *ve-lo hikkiro* — not failed-recognition but **deliberate concealment**, the choice to perform non-recognition. // **The cross-reference to `haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif`.** The companion overlay entry [`haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif`](#haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif) governs the Gen 37 *haker-na* / *va-yakkirah* anchor of the recognition-motif (with the Gen 27 + Gen 38 cross-references documented in its rationale), and has had its appliesTo extended to include Gen 42:7 + 42:8 as the motif's culmination-occurrences. This sibling entry is anchored at the Gen 42:7 paired Hiphil-and-Hithpael deployment specifically (the chapter's Hithpael-of-*nakar* is the motif's anti-form, distinct from the Gen 37 Hiphil-only deployment); the two entries are deliberate companions per the ratified sibling-overlay pattern with bidirectional cross-reference. The motif entry names this sibling by id in its rationale; this entry names the motif entry by id in this paragraph — a true bidirectional sibling link. The pair governs the recognition-arc's full lexical-stem range (the Hiphil disclosure-by-demand at Gen 37; the Hithpael concealment-by-feigning at Gen 42); together they map the motif as it culminates in Gen 42:7-8. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular Hithpael-of-*nakar* construction (the only other HB Hithpael-of-*nakar* occurrence is the 1 Kgs 14:5-6 Achiyah scene); the Gen 27 + 37 + 38 + 42 recognition-arc is Genesis-internal; the chapter-specific Hithpael-pair deployment is here. The companion `haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif` (also overlay-housed) is the Gen 37 anchor. → **OVERLAY** with bidirectional sibling-link to the companion entry. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the paired Hiphil + Hithpael deployment is morphologically explicit; (b) the Hithpael-of-*nakar* feigning-unrecognisability sense is well-attested at the 1 Kgs 14:5-6 parallel; (c) the recognition-motif's Gen 27 / 37 / 38 / 42 cross-chapter structure is textually verifiable; (d) the ASV-baseline 'knew them ... made himself strange unto them' is the direct rendering. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *nakar* (Hithpael); BDB p. 649; TDOT IX:423-432; NIDOTTE 3:107-110; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 107; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 518; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 242; Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1 (the foundational reading of the recognition-arc); on the 1 Kgs 14:5-6 parallel: J. Gray *I & II Kings* OTL 1970 pp. 333-336; on the Yosef-cycle recognition-motif: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975 pp. 130-152.

terms.translit: ha-melitz (the participle of l-w-tz in the 'interpreter / translator' sense, at v 23)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb participle (Hiphil of l-w-tz), here substantivally: 'the interpreter / one who interprets / spokesman / mediator'
terms.literal: ha-melitz — the one who interprets / mediates / speaks-between; here in the 'court interpreter / translator' sense (effectively a hapax in this specific register within the HB)
terms.standardEnglish: an interpreter (ASV/KJV/NJPS/NRSV/Alter — uncontested)
terms.wohChoice: an interpreter between them (ASV-baseline; the lexeme's rare 'interpreter / translator' sense — distinct from the dominant 'scoffer / mocker' sense — documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:23 contains a narrator's parenthetical disclosure: *ve-hem lo yad'u ki shomea Yosef ki ha-melitz beinotam* — *and they knew not that Yosef understood them; for there was an interpreter between them*. The noun *melitz* (מֵלִיץ) here is in the 'court interpreter / translator' sense, which is effectively a hapax in this specific register within the HB. The lexeme's standard senses are quite different — *l-w-tz* otherwise generates the 'scoffer / mocker' (the dominant biblical sense) and the 'mediator / spokesman / advocate' (a secondary sense). The Gen 42:23 'interpreter' deployment is rare and pointed.** // **The lexeme.** The verb *l-w-tz* (or *lits*) has a complex distribution. The Qal participle *letz* and the Hiphil participle *melitz* both appear, with overlapping but distinguishable senses: (i) the dominant **'scoffer / mocker'** sense — Ps 1:1 *u-ve-moshav letzim lo yashav* ('nor sitteth in the seat of the *letzim* / scornful'); Prov 9:7-8 (the *letz* — scorner — who hates correction); Prov 13:1; 14:6, 9; 15:12; 19:25, 29; 20:1; 21:11, 24; 22:10; 24:9; 29:8 — the Proverbs wisdom-literature deploys *letz* as the foil to the wise. The Hiphil *halitz* in this register is 'to scorn / deride' (Ps 119:51 *zedim helitzuni*, 'the arrogant scorn me'; Prov 14:9; 19:28). (ii) The **'mediator / spokesman / advocate'** sense — Job 33:23 (the *malakh melitz*, 'an angel, a mediator', the heavenly advocate in Elihu's speech); Isa 43:27 (*meliteikha pashe'u bi*, 'thy mediators / spokesmen / interpreters have transgressed against me' — possibly the prophets, possibly the priestly intercessors); 2 Chr 32:31 (*melitzei sarei Bavel*, 'the spokesmen / envoys of the princes of Bavel' come to inquire of Hizqiyahu). (iii) The Gen 42:23 **'interpreter / translator'** sense — distinct from the mediator-as-advocate sense by being specifically the language-mediator (the one who renders Egyptian speech into Hebrew or vice versa, the cross-linguistic court interpreter). The Genesis 42 occurrence is the lexeme's only HB attestation in this language-translation register. The semantic relation across the three senses: all share the structure of *one who stands between* — the scoffer stands between truth and the audience (interposing mockery); the mediator stands between two parties (interceding); the interpreter stands between two languages (translating). The Hebrew lexeme captures the 'standing-between' structurally; English distinguishes the three senses by separate words. // **The court-interpreter institution.** The 'interpreter / dragoman' role is well-attested in ancient Near Eastern royal administration. Egyptian-court protocol of the Middle and New Kingdom employed *targumannu*-class language-mediators (the Akkadian term is *targumannu* / *tergumannu*, the Hebrew cognate *targuman*, later Aramaic *targum* — the LXX of Gen 42:23 uses ἑρμηνευτής, the Greek 'interpreter'); the Amarna letters extensively document the use of court-interpreters in royal diplomacy. The Gen 42:23 *melitz* is the Genesis Hebrew rendering of this institutional role. Yosef, the *shallit*, would maintain his Egyptian-court persona by routing his speech to the brothers through the official interpreter — the brothers see only the Egyptian-court-protocol-mediation and do not know that the *shallit* understands their Hebrew directly. // **The narrative disclosure.** The narrator's parenthetical at v 23 is precisely placed: it follows the brothers' v 21-22 confession in Hebrew (the *aval ashemim anachnu al achinu* and Re'uven's *dam nidrash* exchange) and precedes Yosef's v 24 weeping. The reader is told *now* — at the moment the brothers' confession-in-Hebrew has just been recorded — that Yosef has heard everything directly. The brothers, speaking unguardedly in Hebrew, do not know that Yosef has understood; the v 24 weeping follows from the v 21-22 confession Yosef has just overheard. The narrative-architecture is precise: the disclosure of the interpreter's presence makes Yosef's emotional reaction at v 24 narratively grounded. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular 'interpreter / translator' sense; the cross-corpus *melitz* in the 'mediator / spokesman' sense (Job 33:23, Isa 43:27, 2 Chr 32:31) is governed by other contexts when those texts are drafted; the chapter-specific court-interpreter register is here. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit; (b) the chapter-specific 'interpreter' sense is grammatically and contextually clear; (c) the cross-corpus other-senses are documented; (d) the ASV-baseline 'an interpreter between them' is the direct rendering; (e) the court-interpreter institution is well-attested in the ANE-comparative material. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *lutz* (the verb) and *melitz*; BDB pp. 539-540; TDOT VII:547-552; NIDOTTE 2:801-803; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 291; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 111; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 523; on the ANE court-interpreter institution: A. F. Rainey 'The Scribe at Ugarit' *Proceedings of the IAJS* 1969; W. L. Moran *The Amarna Letters* 1992 (the *targumannu* documentation); on the polysemy of *l-w-tz*: M. V. Fox *Proverbs 1-9* AB 2000 pp. 39-43 (on *letz* in wisdom-literature).

terms.translit: kelim ('vessels', v 25); saq ('sack', vv 25, 27, 35); amtachat ('sack-pouch', vv 27, 28; pervasively across Gen 43-44)
terms.partOfSpeech: three nouns alternating across the Gen 42-44 grain-purchase narrative-arc: keli ('vessel, utensil, container'); saq ('sack, cloth-bag'); amtachat ('sack-pouch', restricted to Gen 42-44)
terms.literal: kelim — the general 'vessels / utensils / containers / equipment'; saq — the specific cloth-sack; amtachat — also 'sack', but a distinct lexeme confined within the HB to the Gen 42-44 grain-purchase narrative (Gen 42:27, 28; 43:12, 18, 21, 22, 23; 44:1, 2, 8, 11, 12)
terms.standardEnglish: vessels / sack / sack (ASV/KJV — the alternation flattened in English); bags / sack / sack / bag (NJPS — likewise flattened); generally undistinguished in translation
terms.wohChoice: vessels (kelim) / sack (saq) / sack (amtachat) — ASV-baseline retained; the lexical-distinctness and the possible referential differentiation documented in commentary
terms.rationale: **Gen 42-44 deploys three distinct sack-lexemes — *kelim*, *saq*, *amtachat* — across the brothers' two journeys to Mitsrayim. The alternation is striking and lexically marked, but English translations uniformly flatten the distinction. The third lexeme *amtachat* is the most striking: it is restricted within the HB to the Gen 42-44 grain-purchase narrative (twelve occurrences across Gen 42:27, 28; 43:12, 18, 21, 22, 23; 44:1, 2, 8, 11, 12 — and NOWHERE ELSE in the HB), making it a narrative-arc-specific lexeme.** // **The three lexemes.** (i) *keli* (כְּלִי, plural *kelim*) is the general 'vessel / utensil / container / equipment / weapon' lexeme — extensively distributed across the corpus, covering everything from kitchen utensils (Gen 27:3 Esav's hunting-*keli*; Exod 22:6-7 [MT 22:5-6] vessels lent out) to sacred objects (Exod 25-27, the tabernacle *kelim*) to weapons (1 Sam 17:54 *kelei zeino*, 'his armor'). The lexeme is broad and unspecific. (ii) *saq* (שַׂק) is the specific 'cloth-sack / coarse-cloth-bag' (the same lexeme as the 'sackcloth' of mourning — Gen 37:34 Ya'aqov's *saq*; 2 Sam 3:31; 1 Kgs 21:27; Joel 1:8, 13). The Gen 42-44 *saq* is the brothers' cloth-sack for grain transport. (iii) *amtachat* (אַמְתַּחַת) — the rare lexeme confined to Gen 42-44 — is etymologically obscure; the root has been variously proposed as *m-t-ch* ('to stretch out, to extend') with the *a*-prefix denoting place or means (HALOT registers the etymological obscurity). The lexeme appears to denote a specific kind of sack — possibly a stretched-out / extended cloth-bag, possibly a sub-pouch within a larger container, possibly simply a synonym for *saq*. // **The three explanations of the alternation.** (a) **Referential differentiation**: the lexemes name different containers. The *kelim* are the general travel-vessels (perhaps including jars, leather-bags, etc.); the *saq* is the cloth-sack (the bag); the *amtachat* is a sub-pouch within the bag — supporting v 27's *be-fi amtachto* ('in the *mouth* of his *amtachat*') as referring to a distinct internal compartment, and v 35's *tzeror kasp-o be-saqqo* (his bundle of money in his *saq*) as distinguishing the *saq*-level location from v 28's *amtachti*-level. On this reading the silver was put *in* the *amtachat* (a sub-pouch) which was *in* the *saq* (the outer bag), the bag itself being one of the *kelim* (the general travel-equipment). The reading is supported by Sarna and Westermann as the most likely if a referential distinction is to be drawn. (b) **Stylistic synonymy without referential differentiation**: the alternation is poetic-stylistic variation, the three lexemes being functionally synonymous; the choice between *saq* and *amtachat* at vv 27-28 is variatio for its own sake. The reading is supported by the difficulty of cleanly mapping each lexeme to a distinct referent (especially v 25's *vessels with grain ... money into his sack* — *kelim* and *saq* used in the same sentence for what seems to be the same container). (c) **Source-critical seams**: some commentators (Skinner ICC; Eissfeldt) have read the *saq*/*amtachat* alternation as a documentary-source split (the *saq* the J-source term; the *amtachat* the E-source term, restricted to the E-novella's grain-purchase narrative). The reading depends on the wider source-critical analysis of Gen 42-44 and is not adopted by all commentators. // **The lexeme's restriction to Gen 42-44.** *Amtachat*'s twelve-occurrence distribution exclusively within Gen 42:27, 28; 43:12, 18, 21, 22, 23; 44:1, 2, 8, 11, 12 is one of the corpus's most striking lexical-restriction phenomena. The lexeme is not used elsewhere in Genesis, not used in Exodus or anywhere in the rest of the Pentateuch, not used in the prophets, not used in the wisdom or poetic literature, not used in Chronicles or Ezra-Nehemiah. The restriction is exhaustive. This is the strongest single piece of evidence for either reading (b) the source-critical seam (suggesting the lexeme belongs to one documentary source whose contribution is limited to the Gen 42-44 grain-narrative) or reading (a) the referential-distinction (suggesting the lexeme names a specific sub-container peculiar to the Mitsrayim grain-purchase context). // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV / NJPS / NRSV / Alter all flatten the alternation: *kelim* → 'vessels' (ASV) or 'bags' (NJPS); *saq* → 'sack'; *amtachat* → 'sack' (ASV) or 'bag' (NJPS) — the English distinction between *saq* and *amtachat* is uniformly lost. The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline ('vessels' / 'sack' / 'sack'), with the lexical-distinctness documented in this overlay entry and the per-verse commentary at v 25, v 27, v 35. The English text cannot reproduce the Hebrew's three-lexeme variation without inventing distinctions ('sack-pouch' for *amtachat*) that the standard English translation tradition does not support; the conservative ASV-baseline preservation is preferred, with the apparatus carrying the philological observation. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-arc-specific lexical-alternation (Gen 42-44); the *amtachat* lexeme is exhaustively restricted to this arc; the *saq* and *kelim* lexemes are broadly distributed but the chapter-arc-specific alternation pattern is what is documented here. → **OVERLAY** (the chapter-arc-specific phenomenon; the broader *saq* and *kelim* lexemes would be governed by other contexts in central entries if and when such are warranted). // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the three-lexeme alternation is grammatically and lexically explicit, but (b) the three explanations (referential differentiation / stylistic synonymy / source-critical seam) are interpretive and not decisively resolved; (c) the ASV-baseline rendering flattens the alternation (the philologically more transparent rendering would distinguish, but English convention does not); (d) the *amtachat* lexeme's exhaustive Gen 42-44 restriction is the strongest piece of evidence but does not by itself adjudicate between the three readings. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *keli*, *saq*, *amtachat* (the *amtachat* entry notes the etymological obscurity and the Gen 42-44 restriction); BDB pp. 479 (*keli*), 974 (*saq*), 607 (*amtachat*); TDOT VII:169-175 (*keli*); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 112 (favoring the referential-distinction reading); Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 524; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 320; on the source-critical reading of the *saq*/*amtachat* alternation: J. Skinner *Genesis* ICC 1910 p. 472; O. Eissfeldt *Hexateuch-Synopse* 1922; on the J/E source-analysis of Gen 42-44: G. von Rad *Genesis* OTL 1972 pp. 380-385; for the *amtachat* etymology and the *m-t-ch* root: HALOT s.v. *m-t-ch*; G. R. Driver 'Hebrew Roots and Words' WO 1 (1947-52) 406-415.

terms.translit: malon (here at v 27 in ba-malon, 'in the lodging-place')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine singular (from the root l-w-n / lin, 'to lodge / pass the night')
terms.literal: malon — a place of lodging / overnighting / passing-the-night; a wayfaring stopover (caravanserai, way-station, or night-camp)
terms.standardEnglish: the inn (KJV — anachronistic); the lodging-place (ASV / NRSV); the place where they spent the night (NJPS / Alter)
terms.wohChoice: the lodging-place (ASV-baseline; the wayfaring-stopover / caravanserai sense documented in commentary; the KJV 'inn' anachronism noted)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:27 records the brother's discovery of the restored silver: *va-yiftach ha-echad et saqo lateit mispo la-chamoro ba-malon* — *and as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the* [malon] — he sees the silver in the mouth of his *amtachat*. The noun *malon* names the place where the brothers stopped to spend the night on the return journey to Kena'an.** // **The lexeme.** *Malon* (מָלוֹן) derives from the root *l-w-n* / *lin* ('to lodge, to spend the night, to overnight'), with the *ma-* prefix indicating place or means. The standard formation is *ma- + verbal-root* generating a noun-of-place: *malon* = 'the place of lodging / overnighting'. The lexeme denotes the institutional wayfaring stopover — variously a caravanserai (a roadside enclosure with provision for travelers and beasts), a way-station (a fortified or semi-fortified stop on a trade route), or simply the customary night-camp location for caravans on a given route. The lexeme is NOT 'inn' in the modern Western sense — there were no commercial inns in the modern sense in ancient Near Eastern trade; travelers stopped at caravanserai-style way-stations (often associated with springs, oases, or fortified posts), guest-houses (private or village-provided hospitality), or simply customary camp-sites. The KJV's 'inn' (here and at Exod 4:24, Luke 2:7) is anachronistic and has misled readers; the ASV-baseline 'lodging-place' is the philologically appropriate rendering. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The lexeme recurs at: **Gen 43:21** — the brothers' second-journey *malon* (the same return-journey *malon* type, possibly the same physical location as the Gen 42:27 occurrence); **Exod 4:24** — *va-yhi ba-derekh ba-malon va-yifgeshehu YHWH* — the bridegroom-of-blood encounter (the obscure scene where YHWH meets Mosheh at the *malon* on the way to Mitsrayim, with the Tzipporah-circumcision-and-blood ritual; one of the corpus's most contested passages); **Josh 4:3, 8** — the twelve-stone memorial at Yisrael's *malon* on the night after crossing the Jordan (the camp-site at Gilgal); **2 Kgs 19:23 = Isa 37:24** — Sancheriv's boast of reaching the *malon qitzo* ('the lodging of his border / the night-camp of his furthest extremity', a poetic geographical metonym); **Jer 9:1 [MT 9:2]** — *mi-yittenenni va-midbar melon orchim* ('Oh that I had in the wilderness a *malon* of wayfarers' — Jeremiah's wish for a desert way-station to retreat to away from his people). The cross-corpus distribution is consistent: the lexeme always denotes the institutional wayfaring stopover, never the modern 'inn'. // **The Gen 42:27 narrative context.** The *malon* is presumably a customary night-camp on the route between Mitsrayim and Kena'an — possibly at one of the Negev oases or at a way-station on the desert margin. The brothers stop, one of them opens his *saq* to give the ass its *mispo* (provender), and discovers the silver. The discovery's location at the *malon* is narratively significant: only one brother makes the discovery (vv 27-28), and the dread is collective only later (the full collective discovery at v 35 when they unload their sacks at home). The *malon*-discovery is the first crack in the test, before the home-discovery that completes it. // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus reach (Gen 43:21; Exod 4:24; Josh 4:3, 8; 2 Kgs 19:23 = Isa 37:24; Jer 9:1) but limited distribution; the lexeme is chapter-anchored at the Gen 42:27 discovery-scene narrative point; the cross-corpus reach is documented as a promotion-path. → **OVERLAY** (the lexeme is well-distributed enough that central housing might be warranted on cross-corpus reach grounds; the editorial decision here is to overlay-house with promotion-path noted, since the chapter-narrative-point is what the entry documents). When Exodus is translated, the Exod 4:24 *malon* is the most significant cross-corpus parallel; promotion to central could be reconsidered then. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit; (b) the wayfaring-stopover sense is well-established across the standard lexica; (c) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable; (d) the ASV-baseline 'lodging-place' is the direct rendering; (e) the KJV-anachronism critique is documented in the standard reference works. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *malon* and *lin*; BDB p. 533; TDOT VII:553-555; NIDOTTE 2:790-792; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 524; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 320; on ANE caravan-routes and way-stations: V. H. Matthews 'Hospitality and Hostility in Judges 4' BTB 21 (1991) 13-21; W. F. Albright 'The Egyptian Empire in Asia in the Twenty-First Century B.C.' JPOS 8 (1928) 223-256; on the KJV 'inn' anachronism: J. Jeremias *Jerusalem in the Time of Jesus* 1969 (Luke 2:7 context).

terms.translit: va-yetze libbam (literally 'and their heart went out', at v 28)
terms.partOfSpeech: verbal idiom: verb yatza (Qal 3ms wayyiqtol) + noun lev (with 3mp possessive suffix) — 'their heart went out'
terms.literal: and their heart went out — (idiomatic) the sudden onset of dread / fear / dismay; the courage / life-force draining away
terms.standardEnglish: their heart failed them (ASV/KJV/NRSV); their hearts sank (NJPS / Alter); their heart went out (literal)
terms.wohChoice: their heart failed them (ASV-baseline; the striking literal 'their heart went out' physiological-emotional idiom documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:28 records the brothers' reaction to the discovery of the restored silver at the *malon*: *va-yetze libbam va-yecherdu ish el achiv* — *and their heart went out, and they trembled one to another*. The idiom *va-yetze libbam* (literally 'and their heart went out') is a striking physiological-emotional construction for the sudden onset of dread, fear, or dismay. The construction is rare in the HB and admits two principal readings.** // **The idiom.** The construction 'the heart goes out' (*lev yatza*) is a near-hapax in the HB in this specific physiological-emotional sense. The dominant rendering tradition reads the construction idiomatically as 'the heart failed / the courage drained away' — the heart conceived as the seat of resolve, its 'going out' as the draining of life-force or determination. The reading is supported by the immediate context (the brothers *charadu* — 'trembled'; their fear is the dominant register) and by the parallel idiom *va-yafag libbo* at Gen 45:26 (Ya'aqov, on hearing Yosef is alive, 'his heart fainted'; literally 'his heart grew faint / became cold') — both idioms describe the heart's sudden-shock response to overwhelming news. A more literal reading takes 'the heart went out' as a striking physical image: the heart leaving the body in shock, the imagined-physiological-departure of the life-force at the moment of dread. The literal preservation 'their heart went out' would render the Hebrew image faithfully; the ASV-baseline 'their heart failed them' renders the idiom into the conventional English-equivalent. // **The cross-corpus parallels (the heart-as-seat-of-courage idioms).** The Hebrew Bible deploys several heart-going-out / heart-failing idioms for shock-and-dread: (i) *yatza lev* at Gen 42:28 (this entry); (ii) *pug lev* at Gen 45:26 (the *va-yafag libbo* of Ya'aqov hearing Yosef lives); (iii) *namos lev* ('the heart melts', Deut 20:8; Josh 2:11; 7:5; Isa 13:7; 19:1; Nah 2:11 [MT 2:10] — the most common heart-failing idiom in the corpus); (iv) *namog lev* ('the heart faints', Ps 22:15 [MT 22:14]); (v) *ne'esfu chayyei lev* ('the life of the heart was gathered up', a related sudden-shock construction). The idioms share the structural pattern of *the heart's vital-function ceasing* as the bodily-correlate of sudden-dread. The Gen 42:28 *yatza lev* is the most striking of the cluster — the heart not melting or fainting but going out, leaving the body. The nearest extra-Genesis parallel is **Cant 5:6** *nafshi yatz'ah ve-dabro* — *my soul went out at his speaking* — also a sudden-shock idiom, with *nefesh* ('soul') instead of *lev* ('heart') as the departing-entity. The Cant 5:6 parallel suggests the idiom-type is the *X yatza* (a vital-entity goes out) form. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV/NRSV 'their heart failed them' renders the idiom into the conventional English-equivalent (the 'heart failing' idiom is itself an English-language convention for sudden-dread, e.g., 'his heart failed him at the sight'). NJPS / Alter 'their hearts sank' moves further toward modern register. The literal 'their heart went out' is preserved-in-spirit by the ASV-baseline (the 'failed' captures the failure-of-courage that 'went out' encodes); the literal preservation would be defensible but is rarely adopted because it reads as awkward in English. The ASV-baseline is retained. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular *yatza lev* construction (the only HB occurrence of this specific idiom is Gen 42:28; the cross-corpus parallels are with different vital-entity nouns — *pug lev*, *namos lev*, etc. — and are separate idioms); → **OVERLAY**. The wider heart-failing idiom cluster could receive a future central entry if a cross-corpus collection of the sudden-dread heart-idioms warrants it; the chapter-specific *yatza lev* is here. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the idiom is grammatically and lexically explicit; (b) the heart-as-seat-of-courage sense is direct in the Hebrew physiological-emotional register; (c) the ASV-baseline 'their heart failed them' is the direct idiom-equivalent rendering. The literal-preservation reading is documented as a defensible alternative. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *yatza* (the heart-idiom uses); BDB p. 422; TDOT VI:225-250; NIDOTTE 2:498-502 (yatza); on *lev* in idiomatic constructions: HALOT s.v. *lev*; TDOT VII:399-437 (lev); F. Stolz 'lev Herz' THAT I:861-867; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 113; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 525; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 245; on the Cant 5:6 *nafshi yatz'ah* parallel: M. Pope *Song of Songs* AB 1977; on the heart-failing idiom cluster more broadly: H. W. Wolff *Anthropology of the Old Testament* 1974 pp. 40-58 ('Lev — The Reasonable Man').

terms.translit: tzeror kesef ('bundle of money / pouch of silver', at v 35 in tzeror kaspo and tzeroрот kaspeihem)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun phrase: masculine noun in construct + noun ('bundle of money / pouch of silver')
terms.literal: tzeror kesef — a bundle / pouch / bag of silver; the small money-pouches in which silver coin or weight was carried for commercial transactions
terms.standardEnglish: bundle of money (ASV/KJV/NJPS); bag of money (NRSV); bundle of silver (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: bundle of money (ASV-baseline; the literal 'pouch / bag of silver' sense and the cross-corpus tzeror-cluster documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:35 records the final shock of the chapter: as the brothers empty their sacks at home before Ya'aqov, each finds *tzeror kaspo be-saqo* — *his bundle of money in his sack* — and the brothers and Ya'aqov collectively see *tzeroрот kaspeihem* — *their bundles of money* — and are afraid. The noun *tzeror* (צְרוֹר, 'bundle, pouch, bag') derives from the root *tzarar* I ('to bind up, tie in a bundle'); the construct *tzeror kesef* names the small money-pouches in which silver was carried for mercantile transactions.** // **The lexeme.** *Tzeror* I (from *tzarar* I, 'to bind up') denotes the bundled / tied-up form of whatever is wrapped or pouched. The construct-form *tzeror + (substance)* generates 'bundle of X' compounds: *tzeror kesef* ('pouch of silver'), *tzeror ha-mor* (Cant 1:13, 'sachet of myrrh'), etc. The lexeme is distinguished from *tzeror* II (from *tzarar* II, 'to be narrow / press / oppose'), which gives 'enemy / adversary' senses. The two lexemes are homonymous but etymologically distinct (HALOT registers them separately). // **The cross-corpus *tzeror*-cluster (Gen 42 occurrence and the four parallels).** The lexeme recurs in four notable HB attestations: (i) **1 Sam 25:29** *ve-haytah nefesh adoni tzerurah be-tzeror ha-chayim et YHWH Elohekha* — *and the soul of my lord shall be bound up in the bundle of the living with YHWH thy Elohim* — Avigail's blessing of David. The phrase *tzeror ha-chayim* ('bundle of the living') has entered Jewish liturgical and funerary tradition (the blessing-of-the-departed prayer includes the phrase *te'urar nafsho be-tzeror ha-chayim*, 'may his soul be bound up in the bundle of the living'). The theological-poetic image: the souls of the righteous bound together in YHWH's care, like precious items in a treasure-pouch. (ii) **Prov 7:20** *tzeror ha-kesef laqach be-yado le-yom ha-kese yavo veito* — *he has taken a* tzeror ha-kesef *in his hand; he will come home at the day of the full moon* — the adulteress's husband's traveling money-pouch. The Prov 7:20 *tzeror ha-kesef* is the closest cross-corpus parallel to Gen 42:35: both use the construct *tzeror ha-kesef* for the merchant's traveling money-pouch. The Proverbs occurrence confirms the lexeme's mercantile register. (iii) **Hag 1:6** *u-ha-mishtakker mishtakker el tzeror naquv* — *and he who earns wages earns them into a pouch with holes* — the prophetic indictment of mismanaged commerce; the *tzeror naquv* ('holed pouch') as the image of vain-labor. (iv) **Cant 1:13** *tzeror ha-mor dodi li* — *my beloved is a bundle / sachet of myrrh unto me* — the love-poetry deployment, with *tzeror ha-mor* as the perfume-sachet held between the breasts. The four cross-corpus occurrences plus the Gen 42:35 mercantile occurrence form a tight five-occurrence *tzeror*-cluster: the lexeme covers (a) the mercantile pouch (Gen 42:35; Prov 7:20; Hag 1:6); (b) the metaphorical-poetic bundle (1 Sam 25:29 *tzeror ha-chayim*; Cant 1:13 *tzeror ha-mor*). The Gen 42:35 occurrence is the corpus's earliest narrative-prose mercantile *tzeror* and is the structural anchor of the mercantile-register cluster. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV 'bundle of money' (preserving the literal *tzeror* — the 'bundle' as the bound-up pouch); NJPS 'bundle of money'; NRSV 'bag of money'; Alter 'bundle of silver'. The 'bundle' rendering is awkward in modern English (a 'bundle of money' suggests a sheaf of bills rather than a pouch of silver-weight) but preserves the *tzeror* etymological force; 'pouch of silver' would be philologically more transparent but loses the cross-corpus echo to *tzeror ha-chayim* and *tzeror ha-mor*. The ASV-baseline 'bundle of money' is preserved for the cross-corpus consistency. // **Overlay housing — with promotion-path note.** Cross-corpus reach to 1 Sam 25:29 (the *tzeror ha-chayim* blessing-formula), Prov 7:20 (the mercantile-pouch parallel), Hag 1:6 (the holed-pouch prophetic-indictment), and Cant 1:13 (the love-poetry sachet); the lexeme's reach is genuine. The editorial decision here is to overlay-house the chapter-specific mercantile occurrence, with a promotion-path note: when Samuel or Proverbs or Haggai or Canticles is translated, the lexeme's cross-corpus reach will activate, and promotion to a central *tzeror-bundle-pouch-vocabulary* entry could be considered. The cluster is borderline — five occurrences in five distinct contexts is the cross-corpus threshold; the central-vs-overlay decision is judgment-dependent. For now → **OVERLAY**, with the promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit; (b) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable; (c) the 'bundle / pouch of silver' rendering is the direct sense; (d) the mercantile-register cluster is documented across the standard commentaries. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *tzarar* I and *tzeror* I; BDB p. 865; TDOT XII:339-345; NIDOTTE 3:851-852; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 113; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 526; on the *tzeror ha-chayim* blessing-formula and its liturgical reception: P. K. McCarter *I Samuel* AB 1980 pp. 396-397; on the Prov 7:20 mercantile-pouch parallel: M. V. Fox *Proverbs 1-9* AB 2000.

terms.translit: seivah (here at v 38 in seivati, 'my gray hair / my old age', in the descent-to-She'ol grief-formula ve-horadtem et seivati be-yagon She'olah)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, feminine singular (from sav, 'gray-haired one, elder')
terms.literal: seivah — gray-haired old age, the metonymic noun for old age figured through its bodily marker (the gray hair); 'my gray hairs' figures the patriarch's aged person and life
terms.standardEnglish: gray hairs (ASV/KJV/NRSV); white head (NJPS); gray head (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: gray hairs (ASV-baseline; the metonymic 'gray-haired old age' sense and the Yosef-cycle grief-formula documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:38 records Ya'aqov's striking concrete embodiment of his aged-mourning in the descent-to-She'ol formula: *ve-horadtem et seivati be-yagon She'olah* — *and ye shall bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to She'ol*. The noun *seivah* (שֵׂיבָה) is the metonymic noun for old age figured through its bodily marker (gray hair) — the patriarch's gray hairs standing for his whole aged person and life. The lexeme recurs at Gen 44:29 and 44:31 in the same descent-to-She'ol grief-formula, forming a Ya'aqov-internal repeated grief-arc across Gen 42:38 → 44:29 → 44:31.** // **The lexeme.** *Seivah* (שֵׂיבָה) derives from *sav* (שָׂב, 'gray-haired one, elder'); both lexemes denote the bodily-and-social condition of aged-ness, the *seivah* the abstract / metonymic noun, the *sav* the substantive person. The metonymy is precise: the gray hairs as the visible marker of advanced age stand for the whole aged person. The lexeme is distinct from *zaqen* (זָקֵן, 'old man / elder', the general lexeme for advanced age) and from *yashish* (יָשִׁישׁ, 'aged one', a rarer lexeme); the *seivah* / *sav* pair carries specifically the gray-haired marker, with the social-honor register of the elderly-as-honored that the gray hair calls forth. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The lexeme recurs across the corpus in the standard 'gray-haired old age' register: **Gen 15:15** — Avraham's *titqaver be-seivah tovah* ('thou shalt be buried in a good old age', the patriarchal promise of a long life); **Gen 25:8** — Avraham's death *zaqen ve-saveya yamim*... *be-seivah tovah* ('an old man and full of years... in a good old age'); **Gen 42:38, 44:29, 44:31** — Ya'aqov's *seivah*-and-She'ol grief-formula (three Yosef-cycle occurrences); **Lev 19:32** — *mipnei seivah taqum ve-hadarta penei zaqen* — *before the gray head thou shalt rise up, and honor the face of the old man* — the honoring-the-aged commandment; **1 Kgs 2:6, 9** — Shelomoh's deathbed-instructions about Yo'av (*ve-lo toreid seivato be-shalom she'olah*, 'and let not his gray head go down to She'ol in peace' — the lexical-parallel to Gen 42:38's *horadetem et seivati ... She'olah*, the only HB *seivah* + She'olah cross-corpus parallel) and the parallel about Shim'i; **Deut 32:25** (the Song of Mosheh, lexically related); **Judg 8:32** — Gid'on's death *be-seivah tovah*; **Ruth 4:15** — Naomi's promised restoration *u-khalkel et-seivatekh* ('and a nourisher of thy gray hairs'); **1 Chr 29:28** — David's death *be-seivah tovah*; **Job 41:24 [MT 41:32]** (the Leviathan-and-the-deep poetic deployment); **Ps 71:18** *ve-gam ad-ziqnah ve-seivah Elohim al ta'azveni* — *now also when I am old and grayheaded, O Elohim, forsake me not* — the elder's prayer; **Ps 92:15 [MT 92:14]**; **Prov 16:31** *ateret tif'eret seivah* — *the gray head is a crown of glory* — the wisdom-tradition's honor-formula; **Prov 20:29** *ve-hadar zekenim seivah* — *and the glory of old men is the gray head*; **Isa 46:4** *ve-ad seivah ani esbol* — *and even to your gray hairs will I carry* — the deity's promise; **Hos 7:9** — *gam-seivah zarqah bo* — *gray hairs are sprinkled upon him* — the prophetic indictment of unaware aging. The lexeme is one of the corpus's standard honor-and-age vocabulary nodes. // **The Yosef-cycle Ya'aqov-internal three-fold deployment.** The three Yosef-cycle occurrences (Gen 42:38, 44:29, 44:31) are ALL on Ya'aqov's lips, ALL in the descent-to-She'ol formula (*ve-horadetem et seivati ... She'olah*), and ALL about the fear-of-losing-Binyamin context. The construction is a fixed lament-formula: *seivah* + *She'olah* + descent-verb. The formula's three occurrences (one in Gen 42, two in Gen 44) form a Ya'aqov-internal grief-arc that the 1 Kgs 2:6 cross-corpus parallel echoes lexically (Shelomoh's 'let not his gray head go down to She'ol in peace' uses the same *seivato* + *She'olah* construction in a deathbed-curse register). The Yosef-cycle grief-formula and the 1 Kings cross-corpus parallel are the lexeme's only attestations in the descent-to-She'ol construction. // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus reach (Gen, Lev, Deut, Judg, Ruth, 1 Kgs, 1 Chr, Job, Ps, Prov, Isa, Hos) but Yosef-cycle-anchored grief-formula deployment; the lexeme's cross-corpus reach is genuine and the entry could plausibly be central, but the editorial decision here is to overlay-house the Yosef-cycle-anchored entry (since the chapter-narrative-point is the three-fold grief-formula recurrence in Ya'aqov's mouth), with a promotion-path note: when the Levitical (19:32), Davidic/Solomonic (1 Kgs 2:6, 9), and wisdom (Prov 16:31, 20:29) occurrences are translated, the lexeme's broader honor-and-age vocabulary reach will warrant central housing. → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit; (b) the 'gray-haired old age' metonymic sense is well-established; (c) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable; (d) the ASV-baseline 'gray hairs' is the direct rendering; (e) the Yosef-cycle three-fold deployment is textually verifiable; (f) the 1 Kgs 2:6 *seivah* + *She'olah* construction parallel is documented. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *seivah* and *sav*; BDB pp. 966-967; TDOT XIV:209-217; NIDOTTE 4:1190-1191; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 292-293; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 114; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 527; on the Yosef-cycle *seivah* + *She'olah* descent-formula: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on the 1 Kgs 2:6 parallel: J. Gray *I & II Kings* OTL 1970; on the honoring-the-aged Lev 19:32 commandment: J. Milgrom *Leviticus 17-22* AB 2000 pp. 1664-1667; on *seivah* in the wisdom-tradition: M. V. Fox *Proverbs 10-31* AB 2009.

terms.translit: einennu (negative-existential particle + 3ms suffix: 'he is not [here / present / extant]'; here at vv 13 ve-ha-echad einennu; 32 ha-echad einennu; 36 Yosef einennu ve-Shim'on einennu)
terms.partOfSpeech: negative-existential particle ayin + 3ms suffix; the construction means 'he is not / he is no longer (here / present / extant)'
terms.literal: einennu — 'he-is-not'; the negative-existential 'he is not [here / present / extant]', a charged euphemism for the absence-of-a-person (typically by death or by unexplained disappearance)
terms.standardEnglish: is not (ASV/KJV — literal); is no more (NJPS); is no longer (Alter); is gone (looser)
terms.wohChoice: is not (ASV-baseline literal; the chapter's einennu-refrain across vv 13, 32, 36 documented; the cross-cycle echo to Gen 37:30 and the forward Gen 44:20, 26, 30 noted)
terms.rationale: **Genesis 42 deploys *einennu* (literally 'he is not') four times across the chapter as a deliberate refrain: v 13 (*ve-ha-echad einennu*, 'and one is not' — the brothers' first deployment, in their initial response to Yosef's questioning); v 32 (*ha-echad einennu* — the brothers retelling to Ya'aqov); v 36 (*Yosef einennu ve-Shim'on einennu* — Ya'aqov's climactic double deployment, applying the formula to two missing brothers at once). The refrain echoes Re'uven's anguished *ha-yeled einennu* at Gen 37:30 (the moment Re'uven returned to the empty pit and discovered Yosef gone) and forward-echoes the brothers' Gen 44:20 (*ve-achiv met ... ve-hu levado nishar*), 44:26, and 44:30 deployments before Yosef's final disclosure.** // **The construction.** *Einennu* (אֵינֶנּוּ) is the negative-existential particle *ayin* (אַיִן, 'there is not / is not') with the 3ms pronominal suffix *-ennu*: 'he is not' — denoting the absence-or-non-existence of the referent. The construction is grammatically equivalent to *lo hi shams* ('he is not present') or *einennu po* ('he is not here'). The semantic force is the negative-existential statement of a person's absence, with the particular force of CHARGED EUPHEMISM: the construction does NOT commit to *why* the referent is absent (death? departure? unexplained disappearance?), only that the referent is currently *not*. This deliberate ambiguity is what makes the refrain a literary device in the chapter. // **The chapter-internal refrain's literary force.** The brothers' deployment of *einennu* in vv 13 and 32 is a charged euphemism: they neither admit the sale (the truth) nor state the conventional 'dead' (the false-but-conventional reading they have allowed Ya'aqov to accept). The deliberate non-committal *einennu* preserves the brothers' deception: they say 'he is not' without saying *what happened to him*. Ya'aqov, who has accepted the Gen 37:33 bloodied-tunic evidence, will be the one to state the conventional *met* ('dead') at v 38 (*ki achiv met*) — the brothers will not use the word *met* of Yosef in this chapter. The lexical-restraint is precise: the brothers say *einennu*; Ya'aqov says *met*; the truth (Yosef is alive in Mitsrayim) is known to none of the speakers. // **Ya'aqov's climactic double-deployment at v 36.** Ya'aqov picks up the brothers' refrain and doubles it: *Yosef einennu ve-Shim'on einennu* — 'Yosef is not, and Shim'on is not'. The formula applied to two missing brothers at once (Yosef presumed dead; Shim'on currently bound in Mitsrayim) and threatened toward a third (Binyamin) is the chapter's most concentrated grief-construction. The deployment shifts the refrain's register: the brothers used *einennu* as a euphemistic concealment-device; Ya'aqov uses it as the language of accumulating bereavement — each *einennu* counting another missing son. The threefold count (Yosef + Shim'on + the threatened Binyamin) is the patriarch's grief-arithmetic, and the *alai hayu khullanah* ('all these things are against me') closure seals the lament. // **The cross-Genesis arc Gen 37:30 → 42 → 44.** The refrain begins at Gen 37:30 — Re'uven, returning to the pit to retrieve Yosef and finding it empty, cries out *ha-yeled einennu, va-ani anah ani-va* ('the child is not, and I, where shall I go?'). The Gen 37:30 *einennu* is the first deployment of the refrain in the cycle, in Re'uven's anguished discovery. The refrain returns in Gen 42 (vv 13, 32, 36, four occurrences) as the brothers' deployment and Ya'aqov's double-deployment, and continues forward into Gen 44 (vv 20, 26, 30 — the brothers' deployment before Yosef in the second journey, retelling the same absence-and-loss to the *shallit*-Yosef who is in fact the missing one). The cross-cycle arc Gen 37:30 → 42:13, 32, 36 → 44:20, 26, 30 is one of the corpus's tightest lexical-refrain structures. The arc resolves at Gen 45:3 when Yosef discloses himself: the chapter that has run on the *einennu* refrain is silenced at the *ani Yosef achikhem* disclosure, with *einennu* never again applied to Yosef. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV literal 'is not' preserves the negative-existential force and the deliberate non-committal euphemism; NJPS 'is no more' and Alter 'is no longer' modulate to modern register but lose the construction's stark force. The ASV-baseline literal is preserved across the four chapter-internal occurrences, the Gen 37:30 anchor, and the Gen 44 forward-echoes — the refrain's lexical-keyword status requires uniform rendering. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-internal refrain (four deployments in Gen 42) plus the Gen 37:30 anchor and the Gen 44:20, 26, 30 forward-echoes — the literary arc is Genesis-internal (the Yosef-cycle); → **OVERLAY**. The lemma *einennu* (and the broader *ayin* + suffix construction) is a common Hebrew construction across the corpus; the chapter-specific deployment as the Yosef-cycle missing-brother refrain is what is documented here. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit; (b) the chapter-internal four-fold deployment is textually verifiable; (c) the Gen 37:30 anchor and the Gen 44 forward-echoes are textually verifiable; (d) the deliberate-euphemism reading is documented across the standard commentaries; (e) the ASV-baseline literal 'is not' is the direct rendering. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *ayin*; BDB pp. 34-35; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 290-292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 109, 113-114; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 519, 526; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 243-245 (on the *einennu* refrain); on the Yosef-cycle missing-brother arc: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; G. W. Coats *From Canaan to Egypt* CBQMS 4, 1976.

terms.translit: anokhi e'ervennu (Gen 43:9, Qal imperfect 1cs + 3ms suffix of arav, 'I will be surety for him'); avdekha arav et ha-na'ar (Gen 44:32, the Yehudah-speech repetition)
terms.strongs: H6148 (arav I, 'to pledge, give in pledge, be surety for')
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Qal (with the cognate noun eravon, 'pledge, surety', registered separately in the Gen 38 sibling-overlay entry)
terms.literal: arav — to pledge oneself, to be surety for (another); the verbal action of standing as the pledge-person for another's obligation or safety
terms.standardEnglish: I will be surety for him (ASV/KJV); I myself will be surety (NJPS); I will offer myself as pledge for him (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him (ASV-baseline; the Gen 38 eravon-pledge-triad cross-reference and the moral-literary fulcrum documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:9 stages one of the corpus's most concentrated character-arc moments: Yehudah's surety-pledge to Ya'aqov for Binyamin's safe return — *anokhi e'ervennu mi-yadi tevaqshennu, im lo havi'otiv elekha ve-hitzagtiv lefanekha ve-chatati lekha kol ha-yamim* ('I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him: if I bring him not unto thee, and set him before thee, then let me bear the blame for ever'). The verb *arav* (Qal *e'ervennu*, with the 3ms suffix referring to Binyamin) is the same root as the cognate noun *eravon* (the 'pledge / surety' that Tamar extracted from Yehudah at Gen 38:17-25, governed by the sibling overlay-entry [`eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff`](#eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff)). The Gen 38 → Gen 43 → Gen 44:18-34 Yehudah-arc is widely recognized as the corpus's moral-literary fulcrum: the man who once GAVE a pledge (the *eravon* triad of signet, cord, and staff) for a transaction now OFFERS HIMSELF as the *arav* (the surety-person) for his brother's life.** // **The lexeme.** The verb *arav* I (עָרַב) means 'to pledge oneself, give surety, stand as pledge for another'. The Qal-active is the standard stem for the act of becoming-surety; the cognate noun *eravon* (H6162) names the pledge-object (the security-deposit held until payment). The lexeme is forensically-precise: an *arav* (surety-person) takes responsibility for another's obligation, becoming legally liable if the obligation fails. The construction *anokhi e'ervennu mi-yadi tevaqshennu* — 'I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him' — is the technical surety-formula naming the surety-person and the demand-on-his-hand if the obligation fails. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The verb *arav* in the surety-sense recurs at: **Gen 43:9** (here); **Gen 44:32** (Yehudah's Gen 44:18-34 surety-speech repetition: *ki avdekha arav et ha-na'ar me-im avi le'mor, im lo avi'enu elekha ve-chatati le-avi kol ha-yamim* — 'for thy servant became surety for the lad unto my father'); **Ps 119:122** (*arov avdekha le-tov*, 'be surety for thy servant for good'); **Prov 6:1** (*beni im aravta le-re'ekha, taqa'ata la-zar kappekha* — 'my son, if thou be surety for thy friend'); **Prov 11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26; 27:13** (the wisdom-tradition's repeated surety-warnings against the financial-and-relational risks of standing surety); **Job 17:3** (*sima-na orveni immakh*, 'lay down now, be surety for me'); **Isa 38:14** (Chizqiyahu's *orveni* lament); **Jer 30:21** (the Davidic eschatological figure who *arav et libbo* approaches YHWH). The cognate noun *eravon* in the pledge-object sense is restricted to Gen 38:17, 18, 20 (the Tamar pledge-triad). // **The Gen 38 → Gen 43 → Gen 44 Yehudah-arc.** The arc is one of the corpus's most-cited character-development structures. The Gen 38 scene stages Yehudah's *eravon*-giving: he hands Tamar his personal-identity tokens (the *chotam*, *petil*, *matteh*) as the pledge for the promised *gedi izzim*; Tamar later returns the items via the *haker-na* formula (Gen 38:25, the recognition-formula echoing the Gen 37:32 bloodied-tunic deception that Yehudah architected) and convicts him; Yehudah's *tzadqah mimmeni* verdict (Gen 38:26) names her righteousness. The Gen 38 chapter is therefore one of the corpus's first MAJOR Yehudah-character-development scenes: the man who gave the *eravon* learns from being convicted by it. The Gen 43:9 surety-pledge then re-deploys the same *arav* root in a transformed register: Yehudah now offers HIMSELF as the *arav*, not an external token but his own person. The Gen 44:18-34 surety-speech extends the pledge into the full speech-act that brings the Gen 45:1 recognition-scene: Yehudah's offer to substitute himself for Binyamin (44:33) — 'let thy servant abide instead of the lad a servant to my lord' — completes the transformation. The man who once gave the *eravon* now IS the *arav*; the pledge-taker has become the pledge-person; the man who orchestrated the Gen 37 deception (selling Yosef into slavery) now offers himself into slavery to save the surviving Rachel-line son. // **The bidirectional sibling-overlay link.** This entry is the Gen 43-44 sibling to the existing Gen 38 overlay entry [`eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff`](#eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff). Per the ratified sibling-overlay-entries pattern (Gen 35 / 38 / 39 / 41 / 42 precedents), the two entries are created as SEPARATE companions — NOT by extending one entry's appliesTo — with bidirectional cross-references in each rationale. The Gen 38 entry's rationale has been extended with a 'Cross-references (the Gen 43:9 / 44:32 Yehudah-surety-pledge sibling-overlay link)' paragraph that names this entry by id and documents the Gen 38 → Gen 43 → Gen 44 character-arc. This entry's rationale here cross-references the Gen 38 entry by id. The two entries together govern the *arav* / *eravon* root across the patriarchal narratives. // **The self-imprecatory closing.** *Ve-chatati lekha kol ha-yamim* — literally 'and I shall be sinful before thee all the days' — uses the verb *chatat* (here Qal-perfect-consecutive) in a rare self-curse register. The ASV-baseline 'let me bear the blame for ever' renders the legal-forensic 'bear the blame' force without surfacing the *chatat* lexeme. The literal 'I shall stand sinful before thee all the days' (NJPS variant) preserves the lexeme but reads stiltedly in English. The ASV rendering is preserved; the *chatat* lexeme's broader cross-corpus reach (the standard sin-vocabulary; central anchors at Gen 4:7 *chatat rovetz*, Gen 18:20 the Sedom *chatat*, etc.) is governed elsewhere. // **Overlay housing.** Patriarchal-narrative Yehudah-arc (Gen 38 / 43 / 44) — Genesis-internal sibling-doublet of a load-bearing character-development motif → **OVERLAY** with bidirectional cross-reference to the Gen 38 sibling. The cross-corpus reach into the wisdom-tradition (Prov 6:1 etc.) is genuine but the entry's editorial point is the Genesis-internal Yehudah-character-arc; a future Proverbs translation may justify central promotion if the surety-warnings are governed in unified fashion. → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the verb is morphologically explicit (Qal of *arav*), but (b) the recorded editorial substance is the Gen 38 → Gen 43 → Gen 44 character-arc reading and the moral-literary-fulcrum claim, both of which are interpretive observations between attested readings; (c) the self-imprecatory *chatati lekha kol ha-yamim* rendering is between attested alternatives (the ASV-baseline forensic 'bear the blame' vs. the literal 'I shall be sinful'); (d) the bidirectional-sibling-overlay claim is editorial. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *arav* I; BDB p. 786; TDOT XI:326-329; NIDOTTE 3:495-496; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 268-271, 298, 305-307; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 121-122, 135-137; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 543-545, 562-571; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 322; on the Gen 38 → Gen 43 → Gen 44 Yehudah-character-arc as the corpus's moral-literary fulcrum: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1 ('A Literary Approach to the Bible'); M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; G. W. Coats *From Canaan to Egypt* CBQMS 4, 1976; on the *arav*-as-surety lexeme in ancient-Israelite commercial law: R. Westbrook 'The Phrase 'His Heart Is Satisfied' in Ancient Near Eastern Legal Sources' JAOS 111 (1991) 219-224.

terms.partOfSpeech: verbal idiom: Niphal perfect 3mp of kamar I + noun rachamim (in plural-abstract) with 3ms possessive suffix
terms.literal: nikhmeru rachamav — his rachamim (compassion-affections) burned / grew warm / were stirred — the visceral compassion-yearning construction figured through the burning / warming of the womb-affections
terms.standardEnglish: his heart yearned over (ASV/NRSV); his bowels did yearn upon (KJV — visceral-literal); his feelings for his brother had welled up (Alter); he was overcome with feeling toward (NJPS); his compassion was stirred (modern)
terms.wohChoice: his heart yearned over his brother (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:30; the visceral 'bowels did yearn' KJV-literal and the rachamim womb-root force documented in commentary; the cross-corpus 1 Kgs 3:26 and Hos 11:8 idiom-cluster surfaced)
terms.rationale: **The idiom *nikhmeru rachamav* — 'his rachamim burned / grew warm / were stirred' — is the corpus's most concentrated compassion-yearning construction. The Niphal of *kamar* I ('to be hot, grow warm, burn'; HALOT distinguishes from *kamar* II 'priest', the kemarim of idolatrous priests, a separate lexeme) paired with *rachamim* (the womb-compassion-noun derived from *rechem* 'womb', governed by the central entry [`rachamim-compassion-womb-root`](#rachamim-compassion-womb-root)) generates the idiom. The three HB occurrences (Gen 43:30, 1 Kgs 3:26, Hos 11:8) form a tight cross-corpus *nikhmar*+compassion idiom-cluster, and the Genesis 43 occurrence is the corpus's first.** // **The lexeme.** The verb *kamar* I (כָּמַר) in the Qal is rare; the Niphal (passive-reflexive) is the standard stem for the idiom and means 'to be heated / to grow warm / to become hot / to burn (internally)'. The semantic core is the visceral-physiological sensation of warmth-of-internal-organs: the womb-affections (the *rachamim*) growing-hot in response to a love-or-pity-object. The construction is therefore anatomical-and-affective: the *rachamim* (the womb-affections) burn (the visceral warming) toward (the object of compassion). The lexeme is psycho-physical: the action being described is felt as a warming-of-the-inner-being, the same physical metaphor English preserves in 'my heart went out to', though the Hebrew lexeme is anatomically more specific (the womb-affections, not the heart). // **The three-occurrence idiom-cluster (the cross-corpus parallels).** The construction is restricted to three HB occurrences, each load-bearing: // **(1) Gen 43:30 (here).** Yosef sees Binyamin (his mother's son, the only Rachel-line brother) for the first time in twenty-two years; the construction names the visceral compassion-burning that drives him from the room to weep in private. The deployment is the cycle's most concentrated emotional-marker — the only moment in the cycle Yosef's emotional state is named at this anatomical-visceral register. The compassion-burning is the inner-state; the outward-restraint (the *va-yit'appaq* of v 31, central entry [`yitappaq-emotional-restraint-yosef-arc`](#yitappaq-emotional-restraint-yosef-arc)) is the response. // **(2) 1 Kgs 3:26.** The famous Solomon-judgment scene: the two prostitute-mothers contest the living child, and Shelomoh threatens to cut him in half; the verse names the true mother's response: *va-tomer ha-ishah asher benah ha-chai el ha-melekh ki nikhmeru rachameha al benah va-tomer bi adoni* — 'and the woman whose son was the living child spoke to the king, for her *rachamim* burned for her son; and she said, Oh, my lord'. The construction is VERBATIM identical to Gen 43:30 (same Niphal-of-*kamar* + *rachamim*-with-suffix + *al* + child-object). The Solomon-judgment narrative deploys the construction to identify the true mother by the visceral physiological compassion-response; the false mother's willingness to see the child cut in half is the diagnostic absence-of-the-construction. The construction is therefore the corpus's lexical-anatomical test for the maternal compassion-bond. // **(3) Hos 11:8.** The prophetic deployment, in the divine voice: *eikh ettenkha Ephraim, amaggenkha Yisra'el, eikh ettenkha khe-Adamah, asimkha kitz'voyim; nehepakh alai libbi, yachad nikhmeru nichumai* — 'how shall I give thee up, Ephraim? how shall I deliver thee, Israel? how shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Tzvoyim? my heart is turned within me, together my *nichumai* are burned'. The Hos 11:8 deployment uses the related noun *nichumim* ('compassions / consolations', cognate of *nicham* 'comfort') rather than *rachamim*; the Niphal-of-*kamar* construction is otherwise identical. The deployment names YHWH's compassion-burning-toward-Ephraim in the most concentrated divine-pathos passage of the prophet, and reads as the divine analog of the Solomon-judgment-mother and of Yosef-at-Gen-43:30: the deity's *nichumim* burn toward Ephraim as a mother's *rachamim* burn toward her child. The Hos 11 deployment is one of the corpus's deepest theological-anthropomorphisms; the lexical idiom anchors the maternal-divine compassion-identification. // **The womb-root link.** The *rechem* (womb) → *rachamim* (compassion-noun) derivation makes the construction's force anatomically-precise: it is the *womb-affections* that burn. The 1 Kgs 3:26 occurrence is therefore lexically the most-natural (a mother's womb-affections burning for her womb-born son); the Gen 43:30 occurrence transfers the maternal-anatomical register to Yosef's response to Binyamin (the brother who shares the mother — the only brother on the scene with whom Yosef shares the same womb); the Hos 11:8 occurrence transfers the maternal-anatomical register to the deity-toward-Ephraim. The three deployments draw on the womb-root link in slightly different ways but the construction's semantic-physiological core is consistent. // **The rendering question.** The KJV's 'his bowels did yearn upon his brother' preserves the anatomically-visceral force of the Hebrew (the *bowels* as the modern-anatomical-imprecise-but-visceral approximation of the womb-affections) but reads archaically. The ASV's 'his heart yearned over his brother' modernizes to the heart-as-emotional-organ but loses the womb-root specificity. NJPS 'he was overcome with feeling toward his brother' and Alter 'his feelings for his brother had welled up' are functional moderns that flatten the anatomical force entirely. The ASV-baseline 'his heart yearned over his brother' is preserved for register-consistency; the visceral-anatomical force and the womb-root link are documented in this entry and in the central [`rachamim-compassion-womb-root`](#rachamim-compassion-womb-root) entry. // **The bidirectional sibling-link.** This entry is the Gen 43:30 idiom-specific sibling to the central [`rachamim-compassion-womb-root`](#rachamim-compassion-womb-root) entry. The central entry governs the *rachamim* lexeme's full cross-corpus distribution (the divine-attribute formula Exod 34:6, the Deuteronomic restoration-promises, the prophetic compassion-language, the Psalter, etc.); this overlay entry governs the chapter-specific *nikhmeru rachamav* idiom-construction with its three-occurrence cross-corpus cluster (Gen 43:30, 1 Kgs 3:26, Hos 11:8). The bidirectional cross-reference is wired: the central `rachamim-compassion-womb-root` entry's rationale notes Gen 43:30 as the construction's first attestation; this entry cross-references the central entry by id. The two entries are companions: the central one for the lexeme; this overlay one for the idiom. // **Overlay housing.** The three-occurrence idiom-cluster is genuine cross-corpus reach but the editorial point at Gen 43:30 is the chapter-specific construction-deployment, with the 1 Kgs 3:26 and Hos 11:8 cross-corpus parallels documented as the idiom-cluster. → **OVERLAY** with bidirectional cross-reference to the central [`rachamim-compassion-womb-root`](#rachamim-compassion-womb-root) entry. The construction's three-occurrence restriction makes overlay housing appropriate for the idiom-specific entry; the broader *rachamim* lexeme is housed centrally. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit (Niphal of *kamar* I + *rachamim*); (b) the three-occurrence cross-corpus cluster is exhaustively verifiable; (c) the womb-root etymological link is documented; (d) the maternal-compassion-anatomical reading is established across the standard lexica; (e) the 1 Kgs 3:26 verbatim parallel is grammatically explicit. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *kamar* I (Niphal); BDB p. 485; TDOT VII:153-159; NIDOTTE 2:686-687 (kamar); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 124-125; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 545-546; on the 1 Kgs 3:26 Solomon-judgment lexical parallel: J. Gray *I & II Kings* OTL 1970; on the Hos 11:8 divine-compassion deployment: H. W. Wolff *Hosea* Hermeneia 1974 pp. 202-203; J. L. Andersen and D. N. Freedman *Hosea* AB 1980 pp. 585-589; on the womb-root anatomical-affective register: P. Trible *God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality* OBT 1978 ch. 2 ('Journey of a Metaphor').

terms.translit: hitmahmahnu (Hithpalpel of m-h-h, 'to tarry / delay / hesitate', here at Gen 43:10 in the lulei-counterfactual)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Hithpalpel (intensive-reflexive reduplicated stem) of the root m-h-h
terms.literal: hitmahmah — to tarry, delay, hesitate, linger; the reduplicated Hithpalpel intensifies the simple delaying-action
terms.standardEnglish: lingered (ASV/KJV); tarried (older); had we not dawdled (NJPS); had we not lingered (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: except we had lingered (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:10; the reduplicated Hithpalpel and the eschatological Hab 2:3 cross-corpus parallel documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **The verb *hitmahmah* (הִתְמַהְמַהּ) is the Hithpalpel (intensive-reflexive reduplicated stem) of the root *m-h-h* ('to tarry, delay, hesitate'). The reduplicated stem is a striking morphological feature: the verbal root is doubled (*m-h-m-h*) and conjugated in the Hithpael-with-reduplication pattern, intensifying the simple tarrying-action. Gen 43:10 deploys the Hithpalpel in Yehudah's reproach to Ya'aqov: *ki lulei hitmahmahnu ki ata shavnu zeh pa'amayim* — 'for except we had lingered, surely we had now returned a second time'.
