The counterfactual particle *lulei* ('except / had it not been that') frames the verb in the contrary-to-fact register: the brothers' delay caused the second journey not yet to have happened.** // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The Hithpalpel of *m-h-h* occurs at a small but pointed cluster of attestations: // **Gen 19:16** — *va-yitmahmah* of Lot at Sedom: the messengers seize Lot and his family because Lot is *tarrying* in the doomed city. The Gen 19:16 deployment is the canonical narrative-tarrying scene; the messengers' physical-seizing-of-the-tarrying-one is the structural counterpart of the warning-of-judgment. // **Judg 3:26** — Ehud's escape after assassinating Eglon: *ve-Ehud nimlat ad hitmahmeham* — 'and Ehud escaped while they tarried'. The verbal deployment names the courtiers' delay (whether out of confusion or out of protocol-respect for the king's chambers) that gives Ehud time to escape. // **2 Sam 15:28** — David fleeing from Avshalom, to the priests Tzadoq and Aviatar: *re'u anokhi mitmahmehah ba'avot ha-midbar ad bo davar me'immakhem le-haggid li* — 'see, I will tarry at the fords of the wilderness, until there come word from you to inform me'. The verbal deployment names David's planned tactical-delay at the wilderness-fords. // **Isa 29:9** — the prophetic indictment: *hitmahmehu u-temahu* — 'tarry ye and wonder' (or *hithmemehu u-temahu*; the verbal-form vocalization is debated; some manuscripts read a different root). The Isa 29:9 deployment is the prophets' invitation-or-indictment to the people to engage in their characteristic spiritual-delay. // **Hab 2:3** — the FAMOUS eschatological deployment: *ki od chazon la-mo'ed ve-yafe'ach la-qetz ve-lo yekhazev; im yitmahmah chakeh lo ki vo yavo lo ye'achar* — 'for the vision is yet for an appointed time, and it hasteneth toward the end, and shall not lie; though it tarry, wait for it, because it will surely come, it will not delay'. The Hab 2:3 *im yitmahmah chakeh lo* is the corpus's most-cited eschatological-patience formula — the prophetic instruction to wait-for-the-tarrying-vision. The verse is heavily-cited in the post-biblical Jewish messianic tradition (Maimonides' thirteen principles of faith echo it) and in early Christianity (Heb 10:37 cites it). The lexeme's reach into the prophetic-eschatological tradition is concentrated at this verse. // **Ps 119:60** — *chashti ve-lo hitmahmahti li-shmor mitzvotekha* — 'I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments'. The Psalter deployment names the worshipper's hastening-without-delay in obedience. // **The cross-corpus distribution is therefore moderate but pointed**: a single Pentateuchal occurrence (Gen 19:16 + Gen 43:10), two historical-narrative occurrences (Judg 3:26, 2 Sam 15:28), two prophetic occurrences (Isa 29:9, Hab 2:3 with the eschatological-patience formula), and one wisdom-psalmic occurrence (Ps 119:60). // **The Hithpalpel stem.** The reduplicated Hithpalpel is a relatively rare Hebrew stem-pattern, attested for a small number of roots with internal-iterative or intensive-reflexive force. The *m-h-m-h* reduplication of *m-h-h* names the back-and-forth, hesitating, repeatedly-delaying quality of the tarrying — not a single act of delay but the ongoing-state-of-being-in-delay. The morphological force is therefore precise: *hitmahmah* names the lingering-as-state, the hesitating-as-condition. // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus reach into Pentateuch (Gen 19, 43), historical narratives (Judges, Samuel), prophets (Isaiah, Habakkuk), and psalms (Ps 119) — moderate distribution but limited scope; the chapter-specific Gen 43:10 deployment in the counterfactual-condition is what is documented; the Hab 2:3 eschatological reach noted as a promotion-path-seed. → **OVERLAY** (the lexeme's cross-corpus reach is moderate; central housing is plausible but the editorial point is the chapter-specific deployment with the cross-corpus distribution documented). // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the morphological Hithpalpel is grammatically explicit, but (b) the rendering between 'tarry' (older), 'linger' (ASV), and 'dawdle' (NJPS) is an interpretive choice between attested registers; (c) the eschatological Hab 2:3 cross-corpus parallel is interpretive (the Gen 43:10 mercantile-tarrying does not directly invoke the eschatological-patience register, but the lexical connection is documented). Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *mahmah*; BDB p. 554; TDOT VIII:1-5; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 298; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 121; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 544; on the Hab 2:3 eschatological deployment: J. J. M. Roberts *Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah* OTL 1991 pp. 110-112; on the Hithpalpel stem: J. Joüon and T. Muraoka *A Grammar of Biblical Hebrew* §59h.

terms.translit: mi-zimrat ha-aretz ('of the choice produce / praise-fruits of the land', Gen 43:11)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, feminine singular in construct (from zamar II 'to be choice / strong / praiseworthy', distinct from zamar I 'to sing / make music')
terms.literal: zimrah — choice-produce / pick-of-the-land / praise-worthy fruit; the lexically-distinct zimrah II (from zamar II), separate from the homophonous zimrah I (musical 'song / praise')
terms.standardEnglish: the best fruits in the land (KJV); the choice fruits of the land (ASV); the choice products of the land (NJPS); the bounty of the land (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: of the choice fruits of the land (ASV-baseline; the zimrah I / zimrah II homophonous-lexemes distinction documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **The construct phrase *mi-zimrat ha-aretz* in Gen 43:11 deploys the noun *zimrah* in a 'choice produce' sense that is effectively chapter-singular in this register. The lexeme's analysis is complicated by the existence of a homophonous lemma *zimrah* I ('song / music / praise' from *zamar* I 'to sing'), which is distinct from *zimrah* II ('choice produce / strength / praise-worthy thing' from *zamar* II, a separate root). HALOT registers the two as distinct lexemes; the Gen 43:11 deployment belongs to *zimrah* II.** // **The lexeme.** *Zimrah* II derives from the root *zamar* II — a separate root from the more common *zamar* I ('to sing, make music, praise with song'). The *zamar* II root carries the semantic core of 'to be choice / strong / praiseworthy'; the cognate noun *zimrah* II names that which is choice-or-praiseworthy. The homophonous *zimrah* I ('song / melody / praise' as musical-act) is etymologically unrelated. The two lemmas share the same triconsonantal form and are difficult to distinguish without context. // **The 'choice produce' sense at Gen 43:11.** Ya'aqov instructs his sons to take 'of the *zimrat ha-aretz*' (literally 'of the choice-produce-of-the-land') as the *minchah* for the disguised Yosef. The semantic context unambiguously requires the 'choice produce' sense: the items listed in the verse (balm, honey, spicery, myrrh, pistachios, almonds) are physical-luxury-produce, not songs. The lexeme is therefore the 'choice produce' / 'best of the land' sense. ASV/NJPS/Alter agree on the produce-reading. // **The Exod 15:2 ozzi ve-zimrat Yah debate.** The most-cited HB occurrence of *zimrah* / *zimrat* is at Exod 15:2 (the Song of the Sea: *ozzi ve-zimrat Yah va-yhi li li-shu'ah* — traditionally 'YHWH is my strength and song'). The Exod 15:2 *zimrat* is contested between two readings: (a) *zimrah* I — 'song / praise' (the traditional reading; YHWH as my-song); (b) *zimrah* II — 'strength / might' (some modern critical readings; YHWH as my-strength, doubling the parallel with *ozzi*). The Exod 15:2 occurrence is NOT the Gen 43:11 produce-sense; the two are different lexical-deployments. The Gen 43:11 produce-sense is essentially confined to this verse (with a possible cognate at 2 Sam 23:1 *u-ne'im zemirot Yisrael*, contested as 'pleasant in the songs of Israel' or 'pleasant in the strength of Israel'). The lexical-rarity of the produce-sense is what makes the Gen 43:11 deployment near-hapax. // **The translation choice.** The ASV-baseline 'choice fruits of the land' preserves the produce-reading and is the consensus modern rendering. The KJV's 'best fruits' is functionally equivalent; NJPS 'choice products' modernizes; Alter's 'bounty' loses the lexical specificity. The WoH translation retains ASV. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-near-hapax in the 'choice produce' sense; the Exod 15:2 contested-homophone is governed elsewhere when Exodus is translated. → **OVERLAY** (the chapter-specific produce-sense lexeme; no cross-corpus reach in the produce-register). // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the produce-sense at Gen 43:11 is grammatically explicit from context, but (b) the *zimrah* I / II distinction is interpretive (the lemma-analysis between the homophonous lexemes is a scholarly inference), and (c) the rendering between 'choice fruits' (ASV) and 'bounty' (Alter) is a choice between attested registers. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *zimrah* I and *zimrah* II (the distinct lemma-analysis); BDB pp. 275-276; TDOT IV:91-98; NIDOTTE 1:1116-1118; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 298; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 122; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 544; on the Exod 15:2 *zimrat Yah* contested-homophone: B. S. Childs *Exodus* OTL 1974 pp. 240-244; W. H. C. Propp *Exodus 1-18* AB 1999 pp. 511-513.

terms.translit: kesef mishneh ('double money / second-money', Gen 43:12, 15); mishgeh ('oversight / inadvertence', Gen 43:12, chapter-singular noun)
terms.strongs: H4932 (mishneh, 'double / second / repetition'); H4870 (mishgeh, 'inadvertent error', chapter-singular noun from shagah 'to err inadvertently')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine singular (mishneh in attributive-construct 'double money'); noun, masculine singular (mishgeh, from the root sh-g-h, 'to err inadvertently')
terms.literal: kesef mishneh — money-of-doubling / second-money / double-portion of silver; mishgeh — an inadvertent error / oversight / unwitting fault
terms.standardEnglish: double money (ASV/KJV); a double sum of money (NJPS); double the silver (Alter); peradventure it was an oversight (ASV)
terms.wohChoice: double money (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:12, 15); peradventure it was an oversight (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:12; the chapter-singular mishgeh and the commercial-mishneh sense documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:12 deploys two distinct lexical items in Ya'aqov's instructions about the silver: *kesef mishneh* ('double money', the doubling of the silver for the second journey; recurs at v 15) and *mishgeh* ('an oversight / inadvertence', the chapter-singular noun naming the possible explanation for the silver's return in the brothers' sacks).** // **(i) Kesef mishneh — double money.** The noun *mishneh* (מִשְׁנֶה) spans the corpus in two distinct registers: (a) the simple-doubling / numerical sense — 'double / twofold / second-amount-equal-to-the-first'; (b) the ordinal / office-title sense — 'second [in rank], deputy, vice-regent, substitute'. The Gen 43:12, 15 occurrences belong to register (a): the brothers take *double* the original silver, both to cover the silver mysteriously returned in their sacks AND to fund the second purchase. The doubling-sense recurs at: Gen 41:43 (the office-title *mirkevet ha-mishneh*, governed by the sibling overlay [`mirkevet-ha-mishneh-chariot-of-the-second-gen41`](#mirkevet-ha-mishneh-chariot-of-the-second-gen41) — distinct from the Gen 43 commercial sense); Exod 16:5, 22 (the double-portion of manna for the Sabbath — *lechem mishneh*, the commercial-doubling-as-cultic-provision register); Deut 15:18 (the double-wages-of-a-hired-servant); Deut 17:18 (the king's *mishneh ha-torah ha-zot* — 'a copy of this torah', the ordinal-as-copy register); 1 Sam 8:2 (Shemu'el's second-born son's name); 1 Sam 17:13; 23:17 (David and Yehonatan: *ata timlokh al Yisrael ve-anokhi ehyeh lekha le-mishneh*, 'and I shall be next to thee', the deputy-sense); 2 Kgs 22:14 = 2 Chr 34:22 (Hulda's *mishneh* / second-quarter location); 1 Chr 5:12; 15:18; Jer 17:18 (the prophetic double-destruction: *shivron mishneh shavrem*); Zech 9:12 (*mishneh ashiv lakh*). The lexeme's two registers (doubling vs ordinal/office-title) are differentiated by context; the Gen 43 commercial-doubling deployment is the corpus's first commercial-doubling occurrence. // **(ii) Mishgeh — oversight.** The noun *mishgeh* (מִשְׁגֶּה) is chapter-singular in the HB — it appears only at Gen 43:12. The verbal root *shagah* / *shagag* ('to err inadvertently, to go astray without intention') is the standard Levitical lexeme for inadvertent-sin (the *shogeg* who errs without intention is the subject of the inadvertent-sin sacrificial-rules at Lev 4:2, 13, 22, 27; 5:15, 18; Num 15:22-29). The cognate noun *shegagah* ('inadvertence', the standard Levitical noun) is well-attested in the HB; the *mishgeh* noun-form at Gen 43:12 is morphologically distinct (a different formation from the same root) and is here used in a non-cultic commercial register: Ya'aqov suggests the silver's return may be a *mishgeh* — an inadvertent error / oversight on the part of the Mitsrayim official who handled the transaction. The shift from the cultic-Levitical *shegagah* (inadvertent-sin) to the commercial *mishgeh* (commercial-oversight) is a lexical-register transfer; the same lexical-conceptual frame (unintentional error) is applied across two domains. // **Overlay housing.** Cross-Pentateuchal reach for *mishneh* (Gen, Exod, Lev/Deut, Sam/Kings) but the chapter-specific commercial-doubling deployment at Gen 43:12, 15 is what is documented; the cross-reference to the sibling overlay [`mirkevet-ha-mishneh-chariot-of-the-second-gen41`](#mirkevet-ha-mishneh-chariot-of-the-second-gen41) (which governs the Gen 41 office-title sense) bidirectionally distinguishes the two registers. The chapter-singular *mishgeh* is by definition overlay-housed. → **OVERLAY** for both. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the morphological items are explicit, but (b) the *mishneh* commercial-doubling vs ordinal/office-title distinction is interpretive (the lexeme spans both registers; the chapter-specific deployment is one of two attested senses), and (c) the *mishgeh* / *shegagah* morphological-distinction-but-same-root analysis is interpretive. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *mishneh*, *mishgeh*, *shagah*; BDB pp. 1041-1042 (mishneh), 993 (mishgeh), 993 (shagah); TDOT XIV:307-313; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 298; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 122; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 544; on the Levitical inadvertent-sin code: J. Milgrom *Leviticus 1-16* AB 1991 pp. 226-292.

terms.translit: asher al beito ('him who [is] over his house', Gen 43:16, 19; cf. 44:1, 4)
terms.strongs: H834 (asher, relative particle) + H5921 (al, 'over') + H1004 (bayit, 'house') + 3ms suffix
terms.partOfSpeech: relative-construct idiom: relative particle + preposition + noun-with-suffix; the standard office-title for the chief-of-household / steward / household-administrator
terms.literal: asher al beito — 'he who [is] over his house' — the technical-administrative office-title for the chief steward / household-manager
terms.standardEnglish: the steward of his house (ASV/NJPS); the one who was over his house (literal-functional); the steward (Alter); the chief of his house (some moderns)
terms.wohChoice: the steward of his house (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:16, 19; the cross-corpus royal-administration office-title distribution documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **The idiom *asher al ha-bayit* (or with possessive suffix, *asher al beito*) is the technical office-title for the chief steward / household-administrator across the HB. Gen 43:16, 19 introduces Yosef's chief steward in this technical register; the title recurs at Gen 44:1, 4 (the same official, in the cup-test scene). The idiom is not generic ('someone in his house') but technical (the chief-administrator of the household / palace).** // **The lexeme.** The construction *asher al + (the named entity)* is a standard Hebrew office-naming pattern: 'he-who-[is]-over-the-X' names the X-administrator, the chief-functionary responsible for the X. The *asher al ha-bayit* / *asher al beito* form names the household-administrator; the parallel *asher al ha-tabbachim* (the captain-of-the-guard) and *asher al ha-mashqim* / *ha-ofim* (the chief cupbearer / baker) parallel-constructions name analogous Egyptian-court offices. The lexeme is administrative-technical: it specifies an institutional role, not a casual functional description. // **The Yosef-cycle distribution.** The Gen 43-44 stewardship-scenes deploy the title repeatedly: **Gen 43:16** ('to him that was over his house' — the chief steward receiving Yosef's instructions about the noon-feast); **Gen 43:19** ('they came near to the steward of Yosef's house' — the brothers approaching at the door); **Gen 44:1** ('he commanded him that was over his house, saying' — the cup-test instruction); **Gen 44:4** ('Yosef said unto his steward' — the cup-test execution). The four-occurrence cycle-internal distribution names a specific named-character-by-office: Yosef's chief steward, a recurring figure in the cycle. The earlier Gen 39:4 *va-yifqideihu al beito* — Yosef himself appointed by Potifar 'over his house' — uses a verbal construction with the same al-beito phrase, marking Yosef's own ascent through the household-administration office before his elevation to the *shallit*. The Yosef-cycle's structural irony is that Yosef, who once was the *asher al beito* of Potifar, now has his own *asher al beito*. // **The cross-corpus royal-administration distribution.** The office-title extends across the HB into the royal-administration vocabulary as the chief-minister title under the Davidic-Solomonic and northern kingdoms: **1 Kgs 4:6** (Solomon's officers: *Achisar al ha-bayit*); **1 Kgs 16:9** (Zimri's coup: *Artza asher al ha-bayit*); **1 Kgs 18:3** (Achav's *Obadyah asher al ha-bayit*); **2 Kgs 10:5** (Achav's household-administrator surrendering Shomron); **2 Kgs 15:5** (Yotam *asher al ha-bayit*); **2 Kgs 18:18, 37; 19:2 = Isa 36:3, 22; 37:2** (the famous Elyaqim son of Chilqiyahu *asher al ha-bayit*, against Sancheriv); **Isa 22:15-25** (the prophetic indictment of Shevna *asher al ha-bayit* and the promise of his replacement by Elyaqim — the corpus's most concentrated single-passage treatment of the office, with the key-of-the-house-of-David imagery). The royal-administration deployments name the highest-ranking court official, second only to the king himself; the office carries the keys-of-the-house authority (Isa 22:22's key-of-the-house-of-David image). // **The Egyptian comparative context.** The Egyptian institutional parallel is the *jmj-r3 pr* ('overseer of the house') office attested across the Egyptian administrative corpus; the title was applied to Egyptian household-administrators of all ranks (private estates, royal palace, etc.). The Gen 43 deployment matches the Egyptian institutional context exactly: Yosef's household has an *asher al beito* — an Egyptian-style household-overseer — managing the daily-affairs of his Egyptian estate. The historical-ethnographic plausibility of the Gen 43-44 stewardship-scenes is well-documented in the Egyptological literature (Vergote, Redford). // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus royal-administration reach into the Kings and Isaiah corpus is genuine and substantial; the editorial point at Gen 43:16-19 is the chapter-specific Egyptian-household-context deployment; the Kings / Isaiah / Isa 22:15-25 cross-corpus reach noted as a promotion-path-seed (when those texts are translated, central promotion could be reconsidered for the royal-administration deployment). → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit; (b) the office-title function is established across the standard lexica; (c) the cross-corpus royal-administration distribution is verifiable; (d) the Egyptian institutional parallel is documented; (e) the chapter-internal recurrence is grammatically explicit. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *bayit*; BDB pp. 108-109; TDOT II:107-116; NIDOTTE 1:655-657; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 299; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 122; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 545; on the *asher al ha-bayit* office in the royal-administration: T. N. D. Mettinger *Solomonic State Officials* CB OT 5, 1971 pp. 70-110; J. Begrich 'Sōfēr und Mazkīr' ZAW 58 (1940-41) 1-29; on the Isa 22:15-25 prophetic-treatment: H. Wildberger *Isaiah 13-27* CC, 1997 pp. 365-394; on the Egyptian *jmj-r3 pr* institutional parallel: P. Vergote *Joseph en Égypte* 1959 pp. 24-26; D. B. Redford *A Study of the Biblical Story of Joseph* VTSup 20, 1970.

terms.translit: le-hitgolel ... u-le-hitnafel (the Hithpael-infinitives, Gen 43:18, the brothers' fear-construction)
terms.strongs: H1556 (galal, Hithpael 'roll oneself / fall upon'); H5307 (naphal, Hithpael 'fall oneself / fall upon')
terms.partOfSpeech: two Hithpael infinitives in series; chapter-singular violence-and-pretext construction
terms.literal: le-hitgolel ... u-le-hitnafel — 'to roll [himself] upon us and to fall [himself] upon us' — the Hithpael of galal (rolling oneself / seeking-pretext) paired with the Hithpael of naphal (falling oneself / aggressive-assault) in the corpus's chapter-singular violence-idiom
terms.standardEnglish: that he may seek occasion against us, and fall upon us (ASV/KJV); so that he may seize us as slaves (NJPS — paraphrastic); to throw himself upon us, to fall upon us (Alter — literal)
terms.wohChoice: that he may seek occasion against us, and fall upon us (ASV-baseline; the chapter-singular Hithpael-of-galal + Hithpael-of-naphal violence-pair documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:18 records the brothers' fear-construction as they are brought into Yosef's house: they suppose they are being brought in *al devar ha-kesef ha-shav be-amtechoteinu ba-techillah* ('because of the money that was returned in our sacks at the first time') — *le-hitgolel aleinu u-le-hitnafel aleinu ve-laqachat otanu la-avadim ve-et chamoreinu* — 'to roll [himself] upon us and to fall [himself] upon us and to take us for bondmen, and our asses'. The two Hithpaels in series (Hithpael of *galal* 'roll' + Hithpael of *naphal* 'fall') compose a chapter-singular violence-and-pretext idiom-pair.** // **The lexemes.** (i) **Hithpael of galal** — *hitgolel* — names a 'rolling oneself against' or 'rolling oneself upon' someone, in the aggressive-pretext register. The cognate root *galal* in the Qal names physical-rolling (of stones, of bodies); the Hithpael-reflexive shifts to the metaphorical-aggressive deployment ('roll oneself upon someone' as in physical-or-legal aggression). Cross-corpus the Hithpael is rare in this aggressive sense: 2 Sam 20:12 has *mitgolel ba-dam* of Amasa's body rolling in his blood (a different context); the specifically-aggressive 'seek pretext' sense at Gen 43:18 is essentially chapter-singular. (ii) **Hithpael of naphal** — *hitnafel* — names a 'falling oneself' or 'casting oneself down', with two distinct semantic ranges: (a) the supplicatory-prostration register (Deut 9:18, 25 of Mosheh's intercessory prostration before YHWH; Ezra 10:1 of Ezra prostrating in supplication); (b) the aggressive 'fall upon (as attacker)' register, which is rare in the Hithpael and pointed to here at Gen 43:18. The Hithpael's two registers are differentiated by context; the Gen 43:18 deployment is aggressive. // **The chapter-singular violence-pair.** The two Hithpaels in series — both with the preposition *aleinu* ('upon us') — compose a stylistically-marked violence-idiom. The construction's rarity is precise: the two Hithpaels are individually rare in the aggressive-sense; their paired-series at Gen 43:18 is chapter-singular in the HB. The literary-rhetorical force of the pair is the brothers' compounded-fear: the first Hithpael names the 'rolling-of-pretext' (legal-or-rhetorical accusation), the second names the 'falling-upon' (physical-violent assault). The fear-construction therefore covers both the legal-and-physical violence-threat the brothers anticipate. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV 'that he may seek occasion against us, and fall upon us' captures the legal-pretext + physical-assault force with the conventional English 'seek occasion' for *hitgolel* (a functional gloss). NJPS 'so that he may seize us as slaves' paraphrastically collapses the construction into a single seizure-action, losing the lexical pair. Alter 'to throw himself upon us, to fall upon us' preserves the literal force but at the cost of redundancy in English (the two infinitives are functionally near-synonymous in Alter's rendering). The WoH preserves the ASV-baseline force-and-clarity. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular construction; the two Hithpaels in series do not recur elsewhere; cross-corpus reach for each lexeme is limited (the 2 Sam 20:12 *hitgolel* and the Deut 9:18, 25 / Ezra 10:1 *hitnafel* deployments are different registers). → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the morphological Hithpael pair is grammatically explicit, but (b) the precise semantic registers ('roll-as-pretext' for *hitgolel*; 'fall-upon-as-assault' for *hitnafel*) are interpretive (the lexemes' specifically-aggressive sense at Gen 43:18 is not paralleled elsewhere in the same register), and (c) the rendering between ASV's 'seek occasion' and Alter's literal 'throw himself upon' is a choice between attested approaches. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *galal* (Hithpael), *naphal* (Hithpael); BDB pp. 164-165, 656-658; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 299; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 122; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 545.

terms.translit: matmon ('treasure / hidden store', Gen 43:23; from taman 'to bury / hide')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine singular (from taman 'to hide / bury')
terms.literal: matmon — that-which-is-buried / hidden-store / cache; the standard noun for buried treasure
terms.standardEnglish: treasure (ASV/KJV); a treasure (NJPS); treasure (Alter); buried treasure (some literal)
terms.wohChoice: treasure (ASV-baseline; the buried-and-hidden-store sense and the cross-corpus Isa 45:3 / Jer 41:8 / Job 3:21 / Prov 2:4 distribution documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **The noun *matmon* (מַטְמוֹן) is the corpus's standard 'buried treasure' lexeme, formed from the verbal root *taman* ('to bury, to hide, to conceal') with the *ma-* prefix denoting place or means. The Gen 43:23 occurrence — the steward's reassuring explanation that *Elohekhem ve-Elohei avikhem natan lakhem matmon be-amtechoteikhem* ('your Elohim, and the Elohim of your father, hath given you treasure in your sacks') — is the corpus's first attestation.** // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The lexeme recurs at: **Gen 43:23** (here); **Isa 45:3** — the famous Cyrus-prophecy: *ve-natati lekha otzrot choshekh u-matmonei mistarim, lema'an teda ki ani YHWH ha-qore be-shimkha Elohei Yisrael* — 'and I will give thee the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places, that thou mayest know that I am YHWH, who calleth thee by thy name, the God of Israel'. The Isaian deployment is the lexeme's most-cited prophetic occurrence and names the hidden-divine-treasure given to the Persian conqueror as a recognition-of-divine-providence. The lexical-resonance with Gen 43:23 (the *matmon* given-by-Elohim) is striking. **Jer 41:8** — the *matmonim* hidden in the field: ten men from among the captives at Mizpah plead *al temitenu ki yesh-lanu matmonim ba-sadeh chittim u-se'orim ve-shemen u-devash* ('do not kill us, for we have *matmonim* in the field — wheat, barley, oil, and honey'). The Jeremianic occurrence is the post-destruction concealed-food-supply context. **Job 3:21** — Iyov's lament: *ke-tomenim li-matmonim* ('who dig for *matmonim* more than for hid treasures'). **Prov 2:4** — the wisdom-instruction to seek wisdom *ke-khesef u-kha-matmonim techappesennah* ('as silver, and search for her as for hid treasures'). // **The Gen 43:23 deployment.** The steward's reassurance reframes the silver's mysterious return as a *matmon* — a divine-given treasure, not a Mitsrayim-court accounting-mistake. The lexical choice is theologically loaded: the steward attributes the returned silver to *Elohekhem* (the brothers' deity) rather than to any accounting-explanation or Yosef's secret-instruction. Whether the steward is a Yosef-informed character (the rabbinic-reading) or simply diplomatic, the lexical-choice frames the silver as divine-provision. The construction echoes the broader Yosef-cycle's divine-providence theme (Gen 45:7-8, 50:20). // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus reach into Isaiah, Jeremiah, Job, Proverbs — moderate but limited; the lexeme's most-cited deployment is the Isa 45:3 Cyrus-prophecy, which a future Isaiah translation may make a cross-corpus node. → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-path noted at the Isa 45:3 cross-corpus parallel. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit (the standard *m-* + *taman* formation); (b) the buried-treasure sense is well-established across the standard lexica; (c) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable; (d) the ASV-baseline 'treasure' is the direct rendering. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *matmon*, *taman*; BDB p. 380 (matmon), 380 (taman); TDOT V:367-369; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 299; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 123; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 545; on the Isa 45:3 Cyrus-prophecy and the hidden-treasure motif: J. Blenkinsopp *Isaiah 40-55* AB 2000 pp. 247-253.

terms.translit: va-yitmehu ha-anashim ish el re'ehu (Gen 43:33; Qal imperfect 3mp of tamah, 'to marvel / be astonished')
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Qal (intransitive 'be astonished / marvel'); the chapter-singular impossible-knowledge-recognition scene
terms.literal: va-yitmehu ha-anashim ish el re'ehu — 'and the men marvelled, each unto his fellow' — the brothers' marvel at Yosef's impossible-knowledge seating-by-birthright
terms.standardEnglish: the men marvelled one with another (ASV/KJV); the men looked at one another in astonishment (NJPS); the men were astonished, every man to his fellow (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: the men marvelled one with another (ASV-baseline; the impossible-knowledge seating-by-birthright literary observation and the structural foreshadowing of the Gen 45 disclosure documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:33 stages one of the corpus's most striking impossible-knowledge moments: Yosef seats the brothers *ha-bekhor ki-vkhorato ve-ha-tza'ir ki-tze'irato* — 'the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth' — accurately ranking eleven brothers in birth-order, an act that is impossible knowledge for the disguised Egyptian official. The brothers respond by marveling (Qal *va-yitmehu*) one to another. The verse is mainstream-noted (Sarna, Alter, Sternberg, Fokkelman) as a deliberate identity-hint placed on the surface for the attentive reader — a structural foreshadowing of the Gen 45 disclosure-scene.** // **The lexeme.** *Tamah* (תָּמַהּ) is the corpus's standard 'be astonished / marvel / wonder' verb. The Qal-active is the basic stem; the cognate noun *timhon* ('astonishment') and the cognate adjective *tamuah* are related. The lexeme covers the cognitive-affective response of astonishment at something exceeding-expectation, often with a numinous or unsettling overtone. The semantic core is the 'response-to-the-extraordinary': the *tamah* names the cognitive-affective registration of something-impossible / something-exceeding-the-natural-order. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The verb recurs at: **Gen 43:33** (here); **Isa 13:8** (the prophetic Day-of-YHWH astonishment: *u-tamehu, panim lahavim peneihem* — 'and they shall be astonished one at another; their faces shall be as faces of flame'); **Isa 29:9** (*hitmahmehu u-temahu* — 'tarry ye and wonder', with the *tamah* paired with *hitmahmah*, governed by the sibling overlay entry [`hitmahmah-tarry-delay-hithpalpel-gen43`](#hitmahmah-tarry-delay-hithpalpel-gen43)); **Jer 4:9** (the Day-of-YHWH terror: *yashomu ha-kohanim ve-ha-nevi'im yitmahu* — 'the priests shall be astonished'); **Hab 1:5** (the famous: *re'u va-goyim ve-habbitu ve-hitamhu temahu, ki fo'al po'el bimeikhem lo ta'aminu ki yesappar* — 'behold ye among the nations, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I am working a work in your days which ye will not believe, though it be told you'; cited at Acts 13:41 in the NT); **Ps 48:6 [MT 48:5]** (the kings of the earth astonished at Zion: *hemmah ra'u ken tamahu, nivhalu nechpazu*); **Job 26:11** (Iyov's response to YHWH: *amudei shamayim yerofefu ve-yitmehu mi-ga'arato* — 'the pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his rebuke'); **Eccl 5:7 [MT 5:8]** (the wisdom-text's response to oppression). The lexeme's cross-corpus reach is moderate; its concentrated prophetic-Day-of-YHWH deployment (Isa, Jer, Hab) gives it an eschatological-numinous resonance. // **The Gen 43:33 deployment.** The brothers' marveling-at-the-seating is the narrative's structural identity-hint. Yosef has just seated them with miraculously-accurate knowledge of their birth-order (an act that would require knowing all eleven brothers personally and their relative ages — knowledge no Egyptian official could have). The brothers' marveling-one-to-another is the natural cognitive-affective response; the reader, who knows Yosef's identity, reads the marveling as the brothers' coming-into-proximity-with-the-truth without yet recognizing it. The literary device is widely cited (Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 247-248; Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 ch. 8; Fokkelman 1975). The Gen 45 disclosure-scene resolves what Gen 43:33 has foreshadowed: the brothers' marveling-at-impossible-knowledge will be answered by Yosef's *ani Yosef* self-disclosure. // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus reach (Isa, Jer, Hab, Ps, Job, Eccl) is moderate; the editorial point at Gen 43:33 is the chapter-specific literary-observation (the impossible-knowledge seating-and-marveling as identity-hint), not the general lexeme. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the verb is morphologically explicit, but (b) the recorded editorial substance is the literary-foreshadowing observation (the marveling as identity-hint), which is an interpretive reading widely noted but not grammatically required by the construction; (c) the rendering between 'marvelled' (ASV) and 'astonished' (NJPS / Alter) is a choice between attested registers. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *tamah*; BDB p. 1069; TDOT XV:649-654; NIDOTTE 4:309-310; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 125-126; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 547-548; on the literary-foreshadowing reading of Gen 43:33: R. Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 247-248; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 ch. 8; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on the Hab 1:5 prophetic-deployment: J. J. M. Roberts *Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah* OTL 1991.

terms.translit: mas'ot (Gen 43:34, the stately court-meal portion-lexeme from nasa 'to lift up'; cf. mas'at 'portion')
terms.strongs: H4864 (mas'eit, from nasa, 'to lift up'; the cognate noun for 'portion / lifted-up-thing')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, feminine plural in construct (from the verbal root nasa, 'to lift up, to carry'); names the 'lifted-up-portion' of a feast
terms.literal: mas'ot — lifted-up-portions / things-borne-from-the-host's-table; the stately court-meal lexeme for portions sent from the host's place to the guests
terms.standardEnglish: messes (KJV/ASV — archaic); portions (NJPS / Alter / modern); servings (some moderns)
terms.wohChoice: messes (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:34; the stately court-meal portion-idiom and the broader cross-corpus mas'at-sense documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:34 describes Yosef's stately court-meal hospitality: *va-yissa mas'ot me-et panav aleihem* — 'and he took up portions from before his face [and sent them] unto them'. The noun *mas'ot* (the feminine-plural construct of *mas'eit*) is the stately court-meal lexeme for the portions lifted-up from the host's place at the head of the table and conveyed to the seated guests. The construction 'lift up X from before his face to them' is a court-ceremonial idiom marking the formal-hospitality protocol.** // **The lexeme.** *Mas'eit* (מַשְׂאֵת) derives from the verbal root *nasa* ('to lift up, to carry, to bear'). The *ma-* prefix forms a noun-of-result or noun-of-thing: *mas'eit* = 'that-which-is-lifted-up / that-which-is-borne'. The broader semantic range covers: (a) the stately court-meal portion (Gen 43:34, the present occurrence; 2 Sam 11:8 of David's *mas'at* to Uriyah; Esth 2:18 of Achashverosh's *mas'at* at the royal-feast for Esther); (b) the burnt-offering smoke ('lifted up' from the altar; Judg 20:38, 40 the *mas'eit* of smoke as a battle-signal); (c) the gift / tribute / portion (Jer 38:14; 40:5; Amos 5:11); (d) the lifted-up-hands of prayer (Ps 141:2 *minchat areb mas'at kappai*); (e) the lifting-up of the soul / heart (Lam 3:41); (f) the burden / charge (the responsibility-as-a-thing-borne). The Gen 43:34 deployment belongs to (a): the stately court-meal portion. // **The court-meal context.** The 2 Sam 11:8 parallel is the closest lexical match: David sends Uriyah from the palace to his own house with a *mas'at* — a stately portion from the royal table, intended to honor and disarm. The Esther 2:18 parallel is similar: Achashverosh distributes *mas'at* at the great banquet honoring Esther's elevation. The three deployments (Gen 43:34, 2 Sam 11:8, Esth 2:18) cluster as the stately-court-meal portion-idiom across three royal-court contexts (the Yosef Egyptian-palace; the Davidic monarchy; the Persian royal-court). // **The Gen 43:34 deployment.** Yosef sends portions to his brothers from the host's place at the head of the table; the gesture is the stately-hospitality marker. The narrative-immediately-following observation that Binyamin's portion is *chamesh yadot* (five-fold, governed by the sibling overlay [`chamesh-yadot-fivefold-portion-gen43`](#chamesh-yadot-fivefold-portion-gen43)) marks the differential-favor that the host is publicly displaying — the reader who knows Yosef's identity reads this as Yosef-favoring-the-Rachel-line-brother; the brothers (who do not know) register it as a foreign-court's mysterious-favor. // **The ASV-baseline 'messes'.** The KJV/ASV rendering 'messes' preserves the archaic English court-meal lexeme but is opaque to modern readers ('mess' as a court-portion is obsolete English). NJPS 'portions' and Alter 'portions' modernize. The WoH retains the ASV-baseline for register-consistency; the modernization 'portions' is noted as the natural-modern reading. // **Overlay housing.** The broader *mas'eit* lexeme has cross-corpus reach across the senses listed above; the editorial point at Gen 43:34 is the chapter-specific stately court-meal portion-idiom, with the 2 Sam 11:8 and Esth 2:18 cross-corpus parallels noted. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit, but (b) the specific 'court-meal-portion' sense at Gen 43:34 is one of several attested senses for *mas'eit*, and (c) the rendering between 'messes' (ASV-archaic) and 'portions' (modern) is between attested approaches. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *mas'eit*, *nasa*; BDB p. 673; TDOT X:24-40 (nasa); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 126; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 548; on the 2 Sam 11:8 parallel: P. K. McCarter *II Samuel* AB 1984 pp. 285-286; on the Esth 2:18 parallel: J. D. Levenson *Esther* OTL 1997.

terms.translit: chamesh yadot ('five hands / five portions / fivefold', Gen 43:34)
terms.strongs: H2568 (chamesh, 'five') + H3027 (yad, in the 'portion / share / part' sense)
terms.partOfSpeech: numeral-noun construction: cardinal-number + plural noun in the 'portion / share' sense (the corpus's first 'X yadot' fractional/multiplier construction)
terms.literal: chamesh yadot — five-hands / five-portions / five-shares — the multiplier construction naming a portion five-fold the size of the others
terms.standardEnglish: five times so much as any of theirs (ASV/KJV); five times as much as that of any of the others (NJPS); five times more than the portions of all the rest (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: five times so much as any of theirs (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:34; the chamesh-yadot multiplier construction and the distinct chimmesh fifth-part-fraction lexeme at Gen 41:34 documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:34 records the differential-favor in Yosef's stately court-meal: Binyamin's *mas'at* (the stately court-portion, governed by the sibling overlay [`masot-court-feast-portions-gen43`](#masot-court-feast-portions-gen43)) is *chamesh yadot* — 'five hands / five portions' — greater than that of any of the others. The construction *chamesh yadot* is the corpus's FIRST attested 'X yadot' fractional-multiplier construction; it uses the noun *yad* ('hand') in the specialized 'portion / share / part' sense, qualified by the cardinal-number to express the multiplier.** // **The lexeme *yad* in the 'portion' sense.** The noun *yad* (יָד, 'hand') has a specialized cross-corpus deployment as 'portion / share / part' in distributive-quantity constructions. The semantic transfer from anatomical-hand to 'portion' is metonymic: a 'hand' of grain or money is a unit-portion or a held-quantity. The cross-corpus attestations of the 'yadot' portion-construction are limited but pointed: **Gen 43:34** (here, the first attestation: *chamesh yadot* = five-portions); **2 Sam 19:43 [MT 19:44]** — the men of Israel argue with the men of Yehudah over David's restoration: *eser yadot li ba-melekh* ('I have ten portions / parts in the king'); **2 Kgs 11:7 = 2 Chr 23:8** — the *yadot* divisions of the Levitical guards (the priestly-administrative usage). The construction is the standard idiomatic 'X portions / X shares' form. // **Distinction from the Gen 41:34 chimmesh fifth-part-fraction.** The Gen 41:34 *chimmesh et eretz Mitzrayim* deploys the Piel of the verbal root *ch-m-sh* (the root from which 'five' derives) in a tax-or-administrative sense — 'take up the fifth-part' (ASV) or 'organize-in-fives / organize-in-divisions' (the administrative-reading; governed by sibling overlay [`chimmesh-fifth-part-or-fifth-division-gen41`](#chimmesh-fifth-part-or-fifth-division-gen41)). The Gen 41:34 *chimmesh* deploys the root in the FRACTION sense (one-fifth); the Gen 43:34 *chamesh yadot* deploys the cardinal 'five' in the MULTIPLIER sense (fivefold). The two are lexically distinct constructions sharing only the underlying numeric root. The distinction is important: the Gen 43:34 portion is not 'one-fifth' of someone's portion (which would be smaller) but 'five-times' someone's portion (which is larger). The reader who confuses the two constructions misreads the verse. // **The Gen 43:34 deployment.** The fivefold-portion to Binyamin is the public-honor marker that Yosef displays to the disguised brothers; the differential-favor is meant to be visible. The reader who knows Yosef's identity reads the gesture as Yosef-honoring-the-Rachel-line-brother (the only brother on the scene who shares Yosef's mother); the brothers may be tested by the differential-favor (will they resent Binyamin's favor as they once resented Yosef's *ketonet passim* favor?). The differential-favor's pedagogical function is widely noted (Sarna, Alter): Yosef tests whether the brothers' character has changed since they sold him over Ya'aqov's favoritism. The chapter ends with the brothers drinking and being merry with Yosef (*va-yishtu va-yishkeru immo*, governed by the sibling overlay [`yishkeru-merry-or-drunk-gen9-gen43`](#yishkeru-merry-or-drunk-gen9-gen43)) — apparently without resentment, but the cup-test of chapter 44 will be the definitive resolution. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular construction in the multiplier-sense; the 2 Sam 19:43 cross-corpus parallel governs the cross-corpus 'yadot' portion-construction when Samuel is translated. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the construction is grammatically explicit, but (b) the distinction between the multiplier (fivefold) and fraction (one-fifth) readings is interpretive (the numeric-root is shared with the Gen 41:34 *chimmesh* fraction-construction); (c) the literary-pedagogical reading of the differential-favor as test is interpretive. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *yad*, *chamesh*; BDB pp. 388-389 (yad), 332-333 (chamesh); TDOT V:393-426 (yad); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 126; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 548-549; on the Gen 41:34 / 43:34 numeric-root distinction: J. Skinner *Genesis* ICC 1910 p. 484; on the pedagogical-test reading: R. Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 248.

terms.translit: va-yishkeru ('and they drank / became drunk / were merry', Gen 43:34, Qal of shakhar)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Qal imperfect-with-vav-consecutive 3mp
terms.literal: shakhar — to be drunk / become drunk; the standard intoxication-verb of the HB
terms.standardEnglish: were merry (ASV/KJV — euphemistic); drank their fill (NJPS); got drunk (Alter — literal); were filled with drink (some moderns)
terms.wohChoice: were merry (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:34; the Gen 9:21 Noah-drunkenness echo and the rendering choice between 'merry' (euphemism) and 'became drunk' (literal) documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:34 closes the stewardship-feast scene with the brothers' response: *va-yishtu va-yishkeru immo* — 'and they drank, and were merry with him' (ASV) or 'they drank and became drunk with him' (literal). The verb *shakhar* (Qal *va-yishkeru*) is the standard 'become drunk' verb of the HB. The rendering choice between the euphemistic 'were merry' (ASV/KJV) and the literal 'became drunk' (NJPS/Alter) is a real interpretive decision; the deliberate lexical-echo of Gen 9:21 (Noah's *va-yishkar* — the corpus's first drunkenness, with negative outcome) is a literary observation worth flagging.** // **The lexeme.** *Shakhar* (שָׁכַר) is the corpus's standard intoxication-verb. The cognate noun *shekhar* (the 'strong drink' of the priestly drinking-prohibition Lev 10:9, etc.) names the intoxicating-beverage. The Qal-active means specifically 'to become drunk / be drunk'; the lexeme is NOT the casual-drinking lexeme (which would be *shatah*, the verb of generic drinking) but the intoxication-specific verb. The Gen 43:34 construction pairs *va-yishtu* (the casual-drinking verb, Qal of *shatah*) with *va-yishkeru* (the intoxication verb) — the sequence is 'they drank, and they got drunk'. The pairing makes the intoxication-reading lexically explicit. // **The Gen 9:21 echo.** The corpus's first drunkenness is at Gen 9:21: Noah after the flood plants a vineyard, drinks of the wine, *va-yishkar* ('and was drunk'), and uncovers himself within his tent — the scene leads to Cham's transgression and the cursing of Kena'an. The Gen 9:21 deployment is therefore the corpus's foundational drunkenness-scene, with overwhelmingly negative narrative consequences. The Gen 43:34 *va-yishkeru* is the next attestation of the verb-stem (the Lot-incestuous-drunkenness scene at Gen 19:32-35 uses different verbal constructions — the Hiphil *nashqenu* 'we made him drink' — though it deploys the *shakhar*-conceptual frame). The lexical-echo from Gen 9:21 to Gen 43:34 is striking: the Yosef-cycle's reunion-feast deploys the same intoxication-verb that the post-Flood scene deployed. // **The literary-interpretive question.** The brothers' drinking-to-merry / drinking-to-drunkenness with the disguised Yosef has been read in two registers: (a) **The benign reading** — the brothers' drinking-with-Yosef marks the reunion-festivity, the easing of the morning's terror, the surface-restoration of brotherly fellowship; the rendering 'were merry' (ASV) captures the celebratory tone; the drinking is appropriate to the stately court-meal. (b) **The darker reading** — the brothers' drunkenness (lexically explicit by the *yishkeru*-pairing) is a pre-test condition: the cup-test of chapter 44 will be more decisive in the morning-after. The drunkenness may also re-echo the Gen 9:21 → Gen 19:32-35 narrative-tradition of drunkenness-as-vulnerability (Noah uncovered; Lot's daughters' incest). The Gen 43:34 drunkenness may be the brothers' moment-of-letting-down-their-guard before the cup-test (Gen 44:1-13). The Alter rendering 'they got drunk with him' surfaces the darker reading. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV 'were merry' (euphemistic) preserves the celebratory register without surfacing the intoxication-specificity. NJPS 'drank their fill' modernizes the euphemism. Alter 'they got drunk with him' is literal. The WoH retains the ASV-baseline 'were merry' for register-consistency; the literal-and-darker reading is documented in this entry. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular deployment in the Yosef-cycle; the Gen 9:21 cross-cycle anchor and the Gen 19:32-35 Lot-tradition documented as the literary cross-references; the broader *shakhar* lexeme is well-distributed across the corpus (the priestly Lev 10:9 prohibition; the prophetic indictments of drunkenness; the wisdom-warnings in Proverbs). → **OVERLAY** for the Gen 43:34 chapter-specific deployment with the Gen 9:21 literary-echo. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the verb is morphologically explicit, but (b) the rendering between 'were merry' (euphemism) and 'became drunk' (literal) is between attested approaches, and (c) the literary-echo to Gen 9:21 and the Lot-tradition is interpretive. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *shakhar*; BDB p. 1016; TDOT XIV:701-707; NIDOTTE 4:107-108; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 126; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 549; on the Gen 9:21 Noah-drunkenness as the corpus's foundational drunkenness-scene: D. M. Carr *Reading the Fractures of Genesis* 1996 pp. 102-104; on the pre-test reading of Gen 43:34: R. Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 248; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975.

terms.translit: mah-nitztaddaq (Hithpael imperfect 1cp of tzadaq, 'how shall we declare-ourselves-righteous / clear-ourselves / justify-ourselves', Gen 44:16)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Hithpael (reflexive-declarative) imperfect 1cp
terms.literal: nitztaddaq — to declare-oneself-righteous / clear-oneself / justify-oneself; the rare Hithpael (reflexive-declarative) of tzadaq, naming the speech-act of self-vindication
terms.standardEnglish: how shall we clear ourselves (ASV); how shall we justify ourselves (KJV / more literal); how shall we prove our innocence (NJPS); what can we plead (Alter, functional)
terms.wohChoice: how shall we clear ourselves (ASV-baseline at Gen 44:16; the Hithpael's reflexive-declarative force and the Yehudah-internal Gen 38:26 → Gen 44:16 tzadaq-arc documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 44:16 stages Yehudah's response to Yosef's silver-cup accusation with a rare verbal-form: *mah nomar la-adoni mah nedabber u-mah nitztaddaq* — 'what shall we say unto my lord? what shall we speak? or how shall we clear ourselves?' The verb *nitztaddaq* is the HITHPAEL of *tzadaq* — the reflexive-declarative stem, 'to declare-oneself-righteous / clear-oneself / justify-oneself'. The stem is rare in the HB and is here deployed as the speech-act of self-vindication — the action Yehudah declares the brothers cannot perform.** // **The Hithpael of *tzadaq*.** The verbal root *tz-d-q* generates several stems: the Qal ('to be righteous, be in the right' — the standard stative; the Gen 38:26 *tzadqah* of Tamar is Qal); the Piel ('to declare righteous' — used of human judicial verdicts); the Hiphil ('to declare righteous / vindicate / justify' — the dominant judicial stem, used of both human and divine justification-action); and the rare HITHPAEL ('to declare-oneself-righteous / clear-oneself / justify-oneself' — the reflexive-declarative). The Hithpael's force is precise: not the Qal-state-of-being-righteous but the active speech-act of declaring-oneself-righteous, the rhetorical-juridical attempt to prove-one's-own-innocence. The construction at Gen 44:16 is therefore not 'how can we BE righteous' (Qal) but 'how can we DECLARE OURSELVES righteous' (Hithpael) — the question concerns the rhetorical-juridical act, not the underlying moral state. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The Hithpael of *tzadaq* is rare: **Gen 44:16** (here, the corpus's first attestation) is the only Pentateuchal occurrence. Other principal attestations: the Qal and Hiphil dominate the cross-corpus distribution; the Hithpael is uncommon. The chapter-deployment is therefore distinctively-marked: Yehudah selects the rare stem to name the impossible-speech-act, the self-vindication that the brothers cannot perform. The lexical-choice signals that the issue is not WHETHER the brothers are righteous (a question of being) but WHETHER they can present themselves AS righteous (a question of speaking). // **The Yehudah-internal Gen 38:26 → Gen 44:16 *tzadaq*-arc.** The arc is one of the corpus's tightest Yehudah-character-development structures: // **(1) Gen 38:26 — Yehudah's first *tzadaq* moment.** After Tamar's *haker-na* exposes him, Yehudah declares *tzadqah mimmeni* — 'she is more righteous than I' (or, on the forensic reading, 'she is in the right; the fault is from me'). The Qal-stative declares the comparative-or-forensic verdict in which TAMAR is named righteous and YEHUDAH names himself the one at fault. The Qal-of-*tzadaq* at Gen 38:26 is governed by the existing overlay [`tzadqah-mimmeni-she-is-in-the-right`](#tzadqah-mimmeni-she-is-in-the-right). // **(2) Gen 44:16 — Yehudah's second *tzadaq* moment.** Six chapters later, in the same character's mouth, the Hithpael is deployed: *mah-nitztaddaq*. Yehudah — who once declared TAMAR's righteousness against his own — now declares his BROTHERS' inability to declare themselves righteous before Yosef. The character-arc is exact: the man who once acknowledged another's *tzadaq* now acknowledges the collective brotherhood's inability to perform *tzadaq* for themselves. The lexical-thread Gen 38:26 → Gen 44:16 (both Yehudah-speech-act *tzadaq*-occurrences) is the corpus's tightest Yehudah-internal lexical structure outside the Gen 43 / 44 *arav*-pledge arc. The bidirectional sibling-overlay link to [`tzadqah-mimmeni-she-is-in-the-right`](#tzadqah-mimmeni-she-is-in-the-right) is wired: the Gen 38 entry has been extended with a 'Cross-reference (the Gen 44:16 *nitztaddaq* sibling-overlay link)' paragraph that names this entry by id and documents the Yehudah-tzadaq-arc; this entry cross-references the Gen 38 entry by id. // **The project's third overlay-overlay sibling pair.** The Gen 38 ↔ Gen 44 *tzadaq*-arc joins the ratified Gen 37 ↔ Gen 38 *haker-na* sibling-pair ([`haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif`](#haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif) ↔ [`haker-na-tamar-recognition-gen38`](#haker-na-tamar-recognition-gen38)) and the Gen 38 ↔ Gen 43/44 *arav*-sibling-pair ([`eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff`](#eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff) ↔ [`arav-eravon-yehudah-surety-pledge-gen43-44`](#arav-eravon-yehudah-surety-pledge-gen43-44)) as the project's third overlay-overlay sibling-pair anchored at Gen 38. The three pairs trace the chapter-38 Yehudah-character-arc across three lexical-thematic registers: recognition (haker-na), surety (arav), and righteousness-declaration (tzadaq). Gen 38 is therefore the cycle's anchor-chapter for Yehudah's character-development, with three overlay-overlay sibling pairs marking the chapter's load-bearing function. // **The rhetorical-juridical impossibility.** Yehudah's *mah-nitztaddaq* concedes the collapse of legal-defense: in the face of the silver-cup found in Binyamin's sack, the brothers cannot rhetorically present themselves as righteous; the proof-of-innocence speech-act is unavailable. The concession opens onto the following clause *ha-Elohim matza et-avon avadekha* ('Elohim hath found out the iniquity of thy servants', governed by the new central [`avon-iniquity-cross-corpus-keyword`](#avon-iniquity-cross-corpus-keyword) entry) — the rhetorical-collapse leads to the comprehensive iniquity-confession. The two speech-acts together form the chapter's confession-pivot: the inability-to-clear-themselves leads to the iniquity-found-out. // **Overlay housing.** Genesis-internal Yehudah-character-arc sibling-doublet → **OVERLAY** with bidirectional cross-reference to the Gen 38 sibling. The cross-corpus reach of the broader *tzadaq* root is governed by other entries (the central anchors at Gen 15:6, etc.); the chapter-specific Hithpael deployment in Yehudah's mouth is here. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the Hithpael stem is morphologically explicit, but (b) the rendering between 'clear ourselves' (ASV), 'justify ourselves' (KJV), and 'prove our innocence' (NJPS) is a choice between attested registers; (c) the Yehudah-character-arc reading is interpretive (the Gen 38 → Gen 44 lexical-thread is direct, but the character-development claim is the editorial substance); (d) the deliberate-rhetorical-collapse reading is interpretive. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *tzadaq* (Hithpael); BDB pp. 842-843; TDOT XII:239-264; NIDOTTE 3:744-769; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 305; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 131; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 564; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 333; on the Hithpael of *tzadaq*: B. Johnson 'tzedek' in TDOT XII; on the Gen 38 ↔ Gen 44 Yehudah-character-arc: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1 and *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 211, 264-265; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975.

terms.translit: asher yimmatze ito me-avadekha va-met (Gen 44:9, the brothers' self-imprecatory oath: 'with whomsoever it be found, let him die')
terms.strongs: H4191 (mut, 'to die', here in the imperfect-with-vav-consecutive as an oath-imprecation)
terms.partOfSpeech: self-imprecatory oath-formula: relative clause + finding-verb (Niphal) + suffix + min-particle + collective subject + va-met (the death-imprecation)
terms.literal: asher yimmatze ito me-avadekha va-met — 'with whomsoever of thy servants it [the cup] be found, and [that man shall] die' — the over-broad self-imprecatory oath formula, with the collective enslavement coda ve-gam-anachnu nihyeh la-adoni la-avadim ('and we also will be my lord's bondmen')
terms.standardEnglish: with whomsoever of thy servants it be found, let him die, and we also will be my lord's bondmen (ASV/KJV); whichever of your servants is found in possession of it shall die, and the rest of us shall become slaves to my lord (NJPS)
terms.wohChoice: with whomsoever of thy servants it be found, let him die, and we also will be my lord's bondmen (ASV-baseline at Gen 44:9; the Genesis-internal echo to Gen 31:32 documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 44:9 records the brothers' over-broad self-imprecation in response to the silver-cup accusation: *asher yimmatze ito me-avadekha va-met ve-gam-anachnu nihyeh la-adoni la-avadim* ('with whomsoever of thy servants it be found, let him die, and we also will be my lord's bondmen'). The construction is a marked oath-form: a death-imprecation on the individual whose possession-of-the-object is discovered, plus a collective-enslavement self-imprecation on the rest. The over-breadth (the brothers stake the collective freedom on the supposed-innocence of all) marks the oath as confidently-rash; the literary parallel to Gen 31:32 (Ya'aqov's analogous oath about Lavan's terafim) is striking and documented.** // **The construction.** The oath-formula deploys: (i) the indefinite-relative *asher* introducing the conditional-finding; (ii) the Niphal of *matza* ('to be found') with the 3ms suffix referring to the cup; (iii) the partitive *min* + collective subject *me-avadekha* ('from among thy servants'); (iv) the death-imprecation *va-met* (Qal of *mut*, in the imperfect-with-vav-consecutive used as the oath-conclusion 'let him die / he shall die'); (v) the collective-enslavement coda *ve-gam-anachnu nihyeh la-adoni la-avadim*. The over-breadth is grammatically explicit: the brothers do not say 'whichever of us is found will be enslaved alongside death' but 'let him die AND we also be enslaved' — they stake their freedom on the supposed-innocence of the (singular) finder. The construction is over-confident: in the rare-but-real possibility that the cup is found with one of them, the cost is death plus collective enslavement. // **The Gen 31:32 parallel — Ya'aqov's analogous self-curse.** The literary parallel to Gen 31:32 is one of the corpus's most-noted documentary-internal echoes: when Lavan accuses Ya'aqov of stealing his *terafim* (household-gods), Ya'aqov declares: *im asher timtza et eloheikha lo yichyeh* — 'with whomsoever thou findest thy gods, he shall not live' (Gen 31:32). The parallels with Gen 44:9 are exact: (i) both involve a missing precious-object (Lavan's *terafim* / Yosef's silver-cup) hidden in the youngest-Rachel-line member's possessions (Rachel hides the *terafim*; Binyamin's sack contains the cup); (ii) both invoke a death-curse on the finder that the speaker does not realize will boomerang (Ya'aqov inadvertently curses Rachel; the brothers inadvertently curse Binyamin); (iii) both formulae are over-broad (Ya'aqov says *lo yichyeh*, the brothers say *va-met*); (iv) both contexts involve search-by-status (Lavan's *trial* searches the camp; Yosef's steward searches eldest-to-youngest). The Gen 31:32 → Gen 44:9 echo is widely-noted by named scholarship: the Rachel-line theme (Rachel/Binyamin), the Ya'aqov-and-his-sons-as-deceivers theme, the boomeranging-oath theme. Rachel's death at Gen 35:18 (in childbirth of Binyamin) is often connected to Ya'aqov's Gen 31:32 oath; whether Rachel's death is causally related to the oath is a midrashic-and-modern-interpretive debate (Sarna, Westermann, Alter discuss). The Gen 44:9 brothers' analogous oath might-or-might-not be similarly fatal for Binyamin (the chapter's climax depends on what happens next). // **The literary signature.** The Gen 31:32 → Gen 44:9 pattern is one of the cycle's documented intertextual structures: the same kind of rash-oath sworn by Ya'aqov in his youthful confrontation with Lavan is now sworn by his sons in their confrontation with the disguised Yosef. The pattern's literary force is character-genealogical: the sons inherit the father's rhetorical-rashness, and the cycle's drama depends on whether the inheritance is broken at Gen 44 (whether Yehudah's substitution-speech of Gen 44:18-34 can avert the boomeranging-oath). The literary observation is named-scholarship: Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative*, Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative*, Sarna *JPS Genesis*. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific oath-formula with a documented Genesis-internal echo (Gen 31:32 → Gen 44:9); the broader cross-corpus self-imprecatory oath-vocabulary (chai-X formulae, chalilah-disavowals, etc.) is governed elsewhere; this entry is anchored at the Gen 44:9 chapter-specific construction with the Gen 31:32 echo as literary cross-reference. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the construction is grammatically explicit, but (b) the over-broad / rash reading is interpretive; (c) the Gen 31:32 echo is a literary observation, not a lexical-identity claim; (d) the boomeranging-oath reading is interpretive-narratological. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *mut*; BDB pp. 559-561; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 304; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 130; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 562; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 332; on the Gen 31:32 → Gen 44:9 boomeranging-oath echo: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 and *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 264; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on Rachel's death and the Gen 31:32 oath: N. Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 220 (the Gen 31:32 commentary); for the midrashic and rabbinic readings of the boomeranging-oath: Genesis Rabbah on Gen 31 + Gen 44.

terms.translit: va-yiqre'u simlotam (Gen 44:13; cf. Gen 37:29 va-yiqra et-begadav of Re'uven, Gen 37:34 va-yiqra Ya'aqov simlotav)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Qal imperfect-with-vav-consecutive 3mp + plural noun (the garments)
terms.literal: qara begadim/simlot — to tear the garments / to rend the clothes; the standard HB grief-rending formula performed at the news-of-death / news-of-calamity / discovery-of-loss moment
terms.standardEnglish: they rent their clothes (ASV/KJV); they tore their clothes (NJPS / NRSV); they rent their garments (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: they rent their clothes (ASV-baseline at Gen 44:13; the Yosef-cycle grief-formula triplet Gen 37:29 → Gen 37:34 → Gen 44:13 documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 44:13 records the ten brothers' grief-response to the cup-discovery in Binyamin's sack: *va-yiqre'u simlotam va-ya'amos ish al chamoro va-yashuvu ha-irah* — 'then they rent their clothes, and laded every man his ass, and returned to the city'. The construction *qara + simlot/begadim* (the Qal of *qara* 'to tear, rend' paired with a garment-noun) is the standard HB grief-rending formula performed at the news-of-death / news-of-calamity / discovery-of-loss moment. The Gen 44:13 deployment is the third occurrence in the Yosef-cycle's grief-rending triplet: Gen 37:29 (Re'uven at the empty pit, the cycle's first occurrence — *va-yiqra et begadav*); Gen 37:34 (Ya'aqov on receiving the bloodied tunic — *va-yiqra Ya'aqov simlotav*); Gen 44:13 (the ten brothers at the cup-discovery — *va-yiqre'u simlotam*). The triplet is one of the corpus's tightest cross-chapter grief-formula structures.** // **The lexeme.** The Qal of *qara* ('to tear, rend') in combination with a garment-noun is the standard HB grief-rending formula. The action is performative: the speaker rends his own clothing to physically embody the rupture-of-circumstance, the breaking-of-the-ordinary. The formula's force is ritual: the rending is not casual-tearing but ceremonial-tearing, marking the moment of grief publicly and irreversibly. The verb itself appears in other registers (Hiphil 'tear away', etc.), but the *qara + garment* construction is the grief-formula specifically. // **The Yosef-cycle triplet.** The three occurrences form a deliberate-literary triplet: (i) **Gen 37:29** — Re'uven returns to the pit to retrieve Yosef and finds it empty: *va-yashav el echav va-yiqra et begadav* — 'and he returned unto his brothers and rent his garments'. Re'uven's rending is the cycle's first grief-formula deployment, performed in private discovery-of-loss. (ii) **Gen 37:34** — Ya'aqov receives the bloodied *ketonet passim* and concludes Yosef has been devoured: *va-yiqra Ya'aqov simlotav va-yasem saq be-motnav va-yit'abel al beno yamim rabbim* — 'and Ya'aqov rent his garments, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days'. Ya'aqov's rending is paired with the *saq* (sackcloth) and the *avel* (mourning) lexemes, the corpus's most concentrated grief-cluster. (iii) **Gen 44:13** — the ten brothers at the cup-discovery: *va-yiqre'u simlotam* — 'then they rent their clothes'. The collective-subject distinguishes this third occurrence from the two Gen 37 individual-subject occurrences. The triplet's structural-significance: the three grief-rending occurrences mark the three principal points of the cycle's grief-arc (Re'uven's individual-grief at the pit; Ya'aqov's paternal-grief at the tunic; the brothers' collective-grief at the cup). The brothers as collective-subject in Gen 44:13 is itself marked: the same brothers who once engineered Re'uven's and Ya'aqov's grief now grieve themselves at what they interpret as Elohim's discovery-of-their-iniquity (which Yehudah will articulate at v 16). // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The grief-rending formula recurs as a corpus-wide grief-marker, with the Pentateuchal anchor at Gen 37:29 (Re'uven). The principal attestations: **Num 14:6** (Yehoshua and Kalev rend their garments at the people's rebellion-response to the spies' report); **Josh 7:6** (Yehoshua at Ai's defeat); **Judg 11:35** (Yiftach at his daughter's appearance); **2 Sam 1:11** (David at the news of Sha'ul's death — *va-yachazek David bi-vgadav va-yiqra'em ve-gam kol ha-anashim asher itto*); **2 Sam 3:31** (David at Avner's death); **2 Sam 13:31** (David at Amnon's reported-death); **1 Kgs 21:27** (Ach'av at Eliyahu's curse); **2 Kgs 2:12** (Elisha at Eliyahu's ascent); **2 Kgs 5:7** (the king of Israel at Naaman's letter); **2 Kgs 6:30** (Yehoram at the famine in Shomron); **2 Kgs 11:14** (Athalyah at Yo'ash's coronation); **2 Kgs 18:37 = Isa 36:22** (Elyaqim and Shevna at Ravshakeh's blasphemy); **2 Kgs 19:1 = Isa 37:1** (Chizqiyahu at the same); **2 Kgs 22:11 + 19 = 2 Chr 34:19 + 27** (Yoshiyahu at the Torah-scroll discovery); **Esth 4:1** (Mordekhai at Haman's edict); **Job 1:20** (Iyov at the news of his children's death); **Job 2:12** (Iyov's friends at his appearance); **Jer 36:24** (the contrast — the king and his servants do NOT rend at Yirmiyahu's scroll); **Joel 2:13** (the prophet's reframing — *qiru levavkhem ve-al bigdeikhem*, 'rend your heart, and not your garments', the inward grief-rending). The lexeme is corpus-saturating in the grief-and-mourning register. // **Overlay housing.** The Yosef-cycle grief-formula triplet is Genesis-internal; the wider cross-corpus distribution is genuine and substantial (Num, Josh, Judg, Samuel × 4 occurrences, Kings × 10 occurrences, Chronicles, Esther, Iyov, Jeremiah, Joel) and noted as a promotion-path-seed; the chapter-specific deployment as the Yosef-cycle triplet's third occurrence is what is documented here. → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-seed noted for future Samuel-Kings translation activation. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit (Qal of *qara* + garment-noun); (b) the Yosef-cycle triplet (Gen 37:29 + 37:34 + 44:13) is textually verifiable; (c) the grief-formula function is documented across named scholarship; (d) the ASV-baseline 'they rent their clothes' is the direct rendering; (e) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *qara*; BDB p. 902; TDOT XIII:175-181; NIDOTTE 3:992-993; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 304; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 130; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 562; on the grief-rending formula's cross-corpus distribution: G. Stählin 'Das Bild der Witwe' JAC 17 (1974) 5-20; M. I. Gruber *Aspects of Nonverbal Communication in the Ancient Near East* Studia Pohl 12, 1980; on the Joel 2:13 prophetic-reframing: H. W. Wolff *Joel and Amos* Hermeneia 1977; on the Yosef-cycle triplet: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975.

terms.translit: tarof toraf (paronomastic infinitive-absolute Qal + Pual perfect 3ms of taraf, 'surely [he is] torn in pieces' / 'torn-torn'); Gen 37:33 (Ya'aqov on the bloodied tunic) and Gen 44:28 (Ya'aqov reported-by-Yehudah, the seven-chapter verbatim-echo)
terms.strongs: H2963 (taraf, 'to tear / tear in pieces / rend [by a wild beast]')
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, paronomastic infinitive-absolute + finite-verb construction (Qal infinitive-absolute tarof + Pual perfect 3ms toraf), with the intensifying-emphasis force
terms.literal: tarof toraf — 'tearing he-is-torn' / 'with-tearing he-was-torn' — the paronomastic intensifier construction with the Qal infinitive-absolute + Pual finite-verb
terms.standardEnglish: surely he is torn in pieces (ASV/KJV); he has surely been torn to pieces (NJPS); he has surely been torn by beasts (NRSV); yes, he has been torn to shreds (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: surely he is torn in pieces (ASV-baseline at Gen 37:33 and Gen 44:28; the chapter-pair verbatim echo locking Ya'aqov's continued belief in the Gen 37 false-evidence documented in commentary; the cross-corpus taraf distribution noted)
terms.rationale: **The paronomastic infinitive-absolute + finite-verb construction *tarof toraf* (literally 'tearing he-is-torn') appears twice in the Yosef cycle in Ya'aqov's mouth, seven chapters apart, in verbatim repetition: Gen 37:33 (Ya'aqov's immediate response to seeing the bloodied *ketonet passim*: *chayah ra'ah akhalathu, tarof toraf Yosef* — 'an evil beast hath devoured him; Yosef is without doubt torn in pieces') and Gen 44:28 (Ya'aqov reported-by-Yehudah, the patriarch's continuing-belief: *va-yetze ha-echad me'itti va-omar akh tarof toraf ve-lo re'itiv ad henah* — 'and the one went out from me, and I said, Surely he is torn in pieces; and I have not seen him since'). The verbatim-echo across seven chapters is one of the corpus's most concentrated lexical-cross-chapter structures, locking the patriarch's continued belief in the Gen 37 false-evidence and confirming that the deception has held across the entire intervening narrative time.** // **The construction.** The paronomastic infinitive-absolute + finite-verb construction is the standard HB intensifier (the formula *VERB-Inf + VERB-finite*, here *taraf-tarof + taraf-toraf*, names emphasis-by-cognate-repetition: 'surely / indeed / without-doubt / with-emphasis the action'). The verbal root *t-r-f* ('to tear / tear in pieces / rend [by a wild beast]') generates the Qal active (the wild-beast-as-subject tearing-action), the Niphal/Pual passive (the prey-as-subject being-torn), and several derived forms (the noun *terefah* 'torn-prey / carrion'). The Gen 37:33 + 44:28 construction uses the Pual passive: the prey (Yosef) IS-TORN (passive), not Yosef does-the-tearing. The intensifier paronomasia names the unambiguity of the supposed-tearing: 'surely / without doubt'. // **The Gen 37:33 → Gen 44:28 verbatim-echo.** The seven-chapter cross-chapter verbatim-repetition is the cycle's signature lock-in of Ya'aqov's continued misinformation. At Gen 37:33 the patriarch concludes from the bloodied tunic that Yosef has been killed by a wild beast (the *chayah ra'ah*, governed by the sibling overlay [`chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast`](#chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast)); at Gen 44:28, reported by Yehudah in his great surety-speech, the patriarch is shown to STILL hold the same conclusion — *akh tarof toraf*, 'surely he is torn in pieces'. The lexical-verbatim of the second occurrence (the same *tarof toraf* construction in the same patriarch's mouth) confirms that Ya'aqov has not revised his Gen 37 conclusion in the seven-chapter / twenty-two-year intervening narrative time. The deception has held; the bloodied-tunic-evidence has continued to determine the patriarch's understanding-of-the-past. Yehudah's deployment of the patriarch's words — quoting Ya'aqov's own *tarof toraf* — is part of his rhetorical-strategy: he makes the patriarch's grief audible to the *shallit* (who is in fact the supposedly-torn-in-pieces brother) by reproducing the patriarch's exact words. The reader who knows Yosef's identity hears the dramatic-irony with concentrated force: Yosef hears his father's belief about his death reported by the brother who knows the truth, in the patriarch's own words. // **The cross-corpus *taraf* distribution.** The verb is well-attested in the corpus: **Gen 37:33 + 44:28** (the Yosef-cycle pair); **Exod 22:12** (the law of the borrowed-animal-torn-by-a-beast: *im taroph yittareph yevi'ehu eid, ha-terefah lo yeshallem* — 'if it be torn in pieces, then let him bring it for witness, and he shall not make good that which was torn'); **Jer 5:6** (*aryeh mi-ya'ar hikkam ze'ev aravot yeshoddedem, namer shoqed al areihem kol ha-yotze mehennah yittareph* — 'a lion out of the forest shall slay them, a wolf of the evenings shall destroy them, a leopard shall watch against their cities: every one that goeth out thence shall be torn in pieces'); **Hos 5:14** (*ki anokhi kha-shachal le-Ephraim ve-kha-kefir le-veit Yehudah, ani ani etrof va-elekh* — 'for I will be unto Ephraim as a lion, and as a young lion to the house of Yehudah: I, even I, will tear and go away'); **Hos 6:1** (*ki hu taraf ve-yirpa'enu*, 'for he hath torn, and he will heal us'); **Hos 13:8** (*epgashem ke-dov shakkul ve-eqra segor libbam, ve-okhlem sham ka-lavi, chayyat ha-sadeh tebbaqe'em* — 'I will meet them as a bear bereaved of her whelps, and will rend the caul of their heart, and there will I devour them like a lion'); **Mic 5:7 [MT 5:8]**; **Nah 2:13 [MT 2:12]** (the lion's-den image); **Ps 7:3 [MT 7:2]** (David's plea against pursuing enemies *pen yitrof ke-aryeh*); **Ps 17:12** (*dimyono ke-aryeh yikhsof li-trof*); **Ps 22:14 [MT 22:13]** (the lion-imagery of the psalmist's suffering); **Ps 50:22** (the divine threat); **Job 16:9; 18:4** (the wild-beast-imagery of the divine-anger); **Ezek 19:3 + 6; 22:25 + 27** (the prophetic-leonine imagery of the prophet's people-and-leaders). The lexeme's predominant register is the lion-or-wild-beast-as-subject tearing-action, frequently in prophetic-or-poetic imagery. // **The bidirectional sibling-link to `chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast`.** The companion overlay entry [`chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast`](#chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast) governs the Gen 37 chapter-bracket *chayah ra'ah* construction (the cover-story 'an evil beast hath devoured him' deployed at the cycle's beginning at v 20 and v 33). The Gen 37:33 deployment uses BOTH constructions together: *chayah ra'ah akhalathu, tarof toraf Yosef*; the Gen 44:28 deployment uses only *tarof toraf* in Ya'aqov's retrospective lament. The two overlay entries thus jointly govern the wild-beast-devouring narrative-frame: the *chayah ra'ah* entry for the cover-story creature-naming chapter-bracket; this entry for the *tarof toraf* paronomastic chapter-pair (Gen 37:33 + Gen 44:28). The bidirectional cross-reference is wired: the Gen 37 entry has been extended with a 'Cross-reference (the Gen 44:28 *tarof toraf* sibling-overlay link)' paragraph that names this entry by id; this entry cross-references the Gen 37 entry by id.
